The incorporation of gradient descent-based machine learning methods in Quantum Mechanics is an area with growing research, including the application of two-layer neural networks to approximate Schr\"odinger equation eigenvalues. Nonetheless, the widespread utilization of these methods in real-world applications is hampered by their inability to learn correctly from limited and noisy data due to overfitting issues. The main constraint of many theoretical studies on machine learning lies in their limited broadening of theoretical results to guide practical algorithm development. Our research strives to counter this challenge by analyzing the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks and revealing the circumstances under which they successfully learn and accurately predict quantum eigenvalues despite being trained with limited and noisy data. The findings of our study offer valuable insights that could be useful in developing practical quantum applications using machine learning methods. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations based on cold atom quantum systems. The results show that our theoretical analysis accurately forecasts the experimental outcomes, thereby validating the efficacy of our method. Furthermore, the numerical evaluation highlights the feasibility of achieving satisfactory performance using a surprisingly small and inefficient neural network design. The findings of our study enable the development of machine learning algorithms that can effectively utilize very little and imperfect data to estimate quantum eigenvalues accurately. The incorporation of early stopping also plays a crucial role in the development of our machine learning algorithm, which is capable of achieving high prediction accuracy. Our latest findings provide an update on the extensive anisotropy of cosmic rays recorded at the Pierre Auger Observatory. With over 33,000 ultra-high energy events examined, significant patterns have been found - 14 regions of anisotropy have been identified across 20% of the sky, and we've determined that anisotropies persist up to 8 in scale (R=8°) at the 99% confidence level. Furthermore, the most prominent anisotropy was discovered near the Galactic Center, and we've explored the possibility of associated anisotropies found nearby. Findings also suggest that events above 40 EeV are more evenly distributed than lower-energy events, and the most significant regional anisotropy is centered at right ascension 9.62° and declination -10.07°, with an amplitude of 11%. We've also determined the average intensity of cosmic rays arriving from the Galactic Center to be 3.57±0.42 events per degree squared per year, and have found that events recording an energy >40 EeV are 1.03±0.19 times more frequent than predicted from an isotropic distribution. Finally, the significance of anisotropies was found to decrease with increasing recorded events above 40 EeV, and strategic observations were found to significantly affect our findings - particularly the lack of signals during the night time and under a full moon. These persistent anisotropies remain unexplained and suggest that ultra-high energy cosmic rays may originate from localized, extremely powerful sources. They also imply that cosmic rays are attenuated over relatively short distances - around 25 megaparsecs - as they travel towards Earth. Our findings may be accommodated within the picture of cosmic ray origins that includes "galactic harbors" as proposed in [1]. However, we've found that these anisotropies cannot be fully explained by assuming magnetic field orientation during propagation [2]. Furthermore, we've found that these anisotropies remain unexplained by the model of localized hadronic interactions over extremely large distances [3]. Our findings provide an update on previously discovered anisotropies and the significant patterns we've found encourage continued observation - particularly with the expansion of the Pierre Auger Observatory to the Amaralito site in Mexico. They also encourage further study of the long-distance attenuation and the nature of cosmic ray sources, and the significance of observing multiple signals arriving from the Galactic Center. This paper focuses on solving homogenization problems for two types of thin layers: one is a neighborhood of a minimal surface in a domain D, and the other is a neighborhood of a maximal surface in the product of D with the real line. We use this to derive effective equations for two scenarios: a layer of small thickness surrounding a minimal surface in a domain and a thin layer surrounding a maximal surface. Our approach involves constructing a suitable perturbation of the minimal surface in order to achieve this. 

As an alternative solution, we established in our previous work that for a suite of small layer thicknesses, the homogenization problem for a neighborhood of a minimal surface in a domain can be solved. However, the provided perturbation does not account for cases where the layer thickness may be incommensurable with the surface details. To address this issue, we rely heavily on our general result from our previous work, which allows us to solve the homogenization problem for a suite of incommensurable thin layers by expressing the solution as a sum of two terms: one that solves the homogenization problem for a neighborhood of a minimal surface and another that arises from the interaction between the layer and the surface details. Our result can be generalized to various other thin layer scenarios by using suitable density functions and projections. 

Finally, we illustrate the accuracy of our result with a numerical study of a model involving a thin film of fluid surrounding a sphere, demonstrating how the obtained solution allows us to accurately model the fluid's behavior at very small layer thicknesses. Our method also facilitates the computation of an effective viscosity tensor for the fluid. 

To summarize, we have developed a novel approach to solving homogenization problems for thin layers of incommensurable thickness by constructing a corresponding perturbation of the minimal surface, which allows us to extend our previous results to a broader range of scenarios. Our technique is versatile and can be applied to various other thin layer scenarios, as illustrated by a numerical study of a model involving a thin film of fluid surrounding a sphere. Moreover, our method is both accurate and allows us to compute effective properties at very small layer thicknesses. 

We hope that our work will contribute to the development of a universal perturbation theory that would allow us to obtain a universal and universal perturbation theory that would allow us to obtain precise and universal estimates for the error in the homogenization process.

A quadrupedal robot's ability to navigate and interact in a diverse environment is heavily dependent on an efficient gaits control system. Research in this area has historically been hindered by a lack of uniform movement controllers, making it difficult to apply findings across different robot designs. This paper introduces the Evolutionary Pathway Creator (EPC), a general-purpose controller that can be adapted to various quadruped robots and environments, allowing it to learn an optimal movement strategy through reinforcement learning. By evolving a continuous movement pattern specific to a given robot and environment, EPC enables quadrupedal robots to interact and manipulate their surroundings in a flexible and agile manner. Several EPC-based learning experiments have been conducted across multiple robots and environments, and the resulting controllers have demonstrated improved navigation capabilities and increased robustness compared to prior approaches. Notably, an EPC-trained controller was found to successfully navigate an unstructured environment using an unprecedented gaits pattern, which could also be transferred to a nearby similar environment with minimal adjustments. This research presents a groundbreaking approach to quadrupedal movement control, offering a flexible and universal solution for a diverse range of robots and environments. A long-standing mystery in astrophysics involves the origin of low-temperature (kT ~ 0.3-0.7 keV) gas with high abundance of iron in active galactic nuclei. This paper examines nuclear activity in the center of the Seyfert galaxy NGC\ 7213 using high-resolution Chandra X-ray spectra. Our high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy reveals spatial variations of iron abundance within 1 kiloparsec of the nuclear region. This region contains a soft X-ray component dominated by low-energy emission. We detected significant absorption lines of H-like and lithium-like silicon and magnesium, as well as of helium-like nitrogen, using advanced spectral analysis tools. These findings indicate that the soft X-ray emission is primarily the result of colliding gas with high iron abundance originating from the accretion disk. A warm breeze from the disk is ejecting this gas, with properties such as gas flow rate, speed, and temperature all closely tied to the black hole mass (5.1 +/- 0.3 x 10^6 solar masses). This process is likely common among low-mass active galactic nuclei and may be responsible for the widespread occurrence of warm, iron-rich gas in this category. We have identified a critical dependence of the warm breeze flow rate on the black hole mass. This relationship may hold the key to a broader understanding of the phenomenon in question. Additionally, the soft X-ray emission is not solely produced by a warm breeze or iron-rich gas without nuclear contamination. In fact, the nuclear activity is primarily responsible for the abundant iron observed in the central region of NGC\ 7213. A warm breeze with properties similar to that of NGC\ 7213 is present in the high-resolution Chandra X-ray spectrum of the Seyfert galaxy NGC\ 1068. This phenomenon is not unique to NGC\ 7213 as it also appears in other galaxies such as NGC\ 1068. Furthermore, the central engine of quasars is likely powering iron-rich gas at large distances. Observations of iron abundance in the central region of NGC\ 7213 indicate that relativistic jets do not significantly contribute to this process. However, these jets may deliver iron to the surrounding interstellar medium. In the specific context of NGC\ 7213, iron is primarily delivered to the surrounding interstellar medium via relativistic jets. Advanced actuators in industrial processes can experience exhaustion or restrictions, necessitating the reconfiguration of optimal controllers to direct various low-cost and limited-capacity alternative actuators. Typically, this problem is approached using a model-based reinforcement learning technique called Policy Optimization with Model-based Generative Adversarial Networks. While this method can learn an optimal policy even when the transition model is imperfect and the reward function is approximately known, it has a major drawback: the sample complexity grows exponentially with the number of variables. In an effort to overcome this challenge, we introduce a new framework for model-free reinforcement learning that takes advantage of an existing two-phase reinforcement learning approach. This approach divides reinforcement learning tasks into exploration and exploitation phases. During the exploration phase, agents collect experience using exploration policies, and once enough data is collected, the exploitation policy is learned from these experiences. In this work, we modify the algorithm to allow it to succeed in nonlinear systems, and we demonstrate its efficacy by applying it to reconfiguring the optimal controller of a Constrained Constrained Linear Quadratic Problem. The proposed algorithm is successfully tested in a hard-to-model nonlinear system called Mackey-Glass time series prediction. This model has several variables, which complicates the learning process, but our algorithm is capable of handling complex systems effectively. In addition to these tests, we successfully demonstrate the applicability of the model-free reinforcement learning algorithm in a real-world use case involving an actual industrial device. This device is called an anomaly and is part of a system called Temperature Tuning Via Electrical Resistance which tunes temperatures using electrical resistance. The device experiences a persistent problem called thermal overload and our model is capable of helping it by reconfiguring its controller using a reinforcement learning technique called Policy Optimization with Model-based Generative Adversarial Networks. The results of our tests show that our model is successful in reconfiguring the controller and helping the device operate more efficiently. This efficiency is measured using a reinforcement learning metric called return and our model is able to increase this return by a significant amount, which indicates that it is operating at maximum capacity. The model consists of 5982 parameters, and when we increased the number of variables in the system by which the device operates, the model was capable of adapting and achieving high returns. This capability is known as generalizability and our model exhibits it successfully. The proposed algorithm is quite efficient as it only requires about 4500 experiences to learn an optimal policy in a complex system with many variables. We introduce a new wide-field view of Tonantzintla 2, a highly variable star system located in the Milky Way's bulge, captured through data from the VVVX and Gaia projects. We obtained spectra for 14 stars within 5 arcminutes of Tonantzintla 2, revealing 7 anomalous Cepheids, 5 red clump stars, and 2 other stars. We measured Cepheid periods and identified 2 new ones with lengths of 10.410 and 20.110 days. We calculated absolute magnitudes and distances for these Cepheids, along with other Tonantzintla 2 stars, using Gaia data. Further analysis revealed Tonantzintla 2 to be an overlapping double star system comprising a red giant and a white dwarf, with the presence of dust due to interaction between the components. We observed variability in additional stars within the field, specifically 3 red giants and 3 red dwarfs, primarily attributed to stellar pulsation. Our study significantly expands the observed variability and physical properties of this region. A detailed analysis of Tonantzintla 2's light curves is underway, while further research on the system's peculiar characteristics is expected to be beneficial. The data presented here will be made publicly available through the VSA portal. We have designated the fiducial star as J194914.14-744936.8, with an initial period estimation strategy. Our study is the third in a series, with the first published in Klimek et al. (2020), and is continuing with data analysis in Vivas et al. (subsubmitted). By simulating how these equations evolve under various parameters, researchers found a phase transition from a homogeneous to a nonlinear state as the system becomes increasingly non-linear. However, this phase transition differs from traditional ferromagnetic transitions in that it's not accompanied by a clear zero-point transition in a specific direction. Rather, the zero-point transition is only evident when incorporating higher higher-point correlations specific to active nematic systems in the renormalization group simulation. Furthermore, the study finds that the dynamics of the system near the zero-point transition share similarities with glassy dynamics, characterized by slow, power-law decay. The work offers a methodological framework for using the renormalization group to analyze hydrodynamic theories and predicts unique behavior in active nematic systems due to their unique blend of geodesic and active forces. Since current experimental techniques can't distinguish a zero-point transition, the study suggests looking into the distribution of relaxation times in experiments to identify signs of the zero-point transition. Additionally, the proposed framework may aid further research even if the zero-point transition can't be observed. The authors provide theoretical predictions for specific correlation functions and scattering patterns that could be tested in future experiments. These predictions include specific relationships between different terms in a correlation function that are characteristic of active nematic systems and a particular scaling behavior in scattering patterns as the unlinear parameter increases. The study also discusses how to modify the active nematic hydrodynamics equations to better match experimental observations and suggests specific changes based on the renormalization group simulation. Overall, the researchers conclude that the zero-point transition is an intrinsic part of active nematic systems and using the renormalization group to study their dynamics is a viable approach. Furthermore, the predicted behavior of the system near the zero-point transition, particularly the distribution of relaxation times, should be observable in experiments once techniques allow for resolving this timescale. The study suggests that the nonlinear behavior of active nematic systems is a result of their inherent zero-point transition and the unique blend of their governing equations. Although this transition may not be directly observable with current techniques, the predicted changes in the distribution of relaxation times and the behavior of the system near the zero-point transition should be testable in future experiments once better resolution allows viewing these effects. Lastly, the study proposes adjusting the active nematic hydrodynamics equations to better match these predicted observations, providing specific predictions and modifications that could be tested in future experiments. The reconstruction of activity dynamics from electroencephalography (EEG) signals has long been a primary objective in EEG analysis. Researchers aim to uncover underlying processes driving signal variations to further understand cognitive functions and disorders.  Identifying anomalies in signal patterns is another key goal as they may contain insights into unusual states or events. Most current methods focus on detecting anomalies within fixed time windows or signal segments.  Conversely, this study proposes a novel framework, referred to as ReAD, which identifies anomalies within continuous time frames by analyzing the context and ongoing processes.  ReAD employs a dynamic segmentation approach to analyze various segment sizes and correlates anomalies across segments using both deterministic and learning-based comparisons.  The framework's efficacy was validated in simulations and clinical applications involving EEG signals from individuals with rare neurological disorders, where researchers aimed to identify distinct anomaly patterns to inform diagnosis and treatment.  Ultimately, ReAD successfully detected subtle anomalies and extracted rare signal patterns that could inform clinical decisions with potential for broader use in EEG analysis.  The framework may be applied to other types of data, such as time series data, for feature reduction and extracting relevant information.  The source code for ReAD is available at https://github.com/NICUSolutions/ReAD.  The dataset used in this study can be accessed through the database of uncaliquated epilepsy patients maintained by the National Institute of Clinical University.  Information on clinical and EEG data collection, as well as data sharing practices, is available at https://intrinca.github.io/epiXML/.  The current version of ReAD supports analysis of EEG signals, but future enhancements will include support for other types of data.  Future work will focus on integrating the variables into ReAD for joint anomaly detection and extraction of underlying features.  Additionally, the impact of using learned anomalies will be investigated.  Future research may also involve comparing the efficacy of ReAD with other state-of-the-art methods, particularly those using deep learning models.  Future work may also involve investigating the applicability of ReAD in cross-domain studies and extending its use to other types of signals, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) signals, for joint anomaly detection.  Finally, the anomaly detection approach employed in ReAD may be further developed into a more general method for identifying anomalies in continuous time signals. We've derived a novel parameterization of the pion vector form factor, utilizing latest lattice QCD data and radiative decays, to better comprehend the vector form factor and its contributions to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. This new parameterization exhibits excellent agreement with numerous lattice QCD studies. Furthermore, we've assessed several vector meson exchange models, revealing that the $\rho$ and f1 mesons significantly affect the pion exchange, while the $\phi$ meson has a minimal impact. Moreover, we've found that the total hadronic contribution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, derived from the (g-2) experiment's 2020 results combined with recent lattice QCD data, could be as high as $(1.5 \pm 0.5) \times 10^{-9}$. This might resolve the discrepancy between the observed and predicted results. Our findings also suggest the need for precise measurements of the f1 vector meson to enhance pion physics understanding. Our work has been made accessible through public archiving. We've also provided the necessary computer code to reproduce our results and facilitate future applications. This includes the code for the pion vector form factor and its associated uncertainties, as well as code for evaluating the muon's anomalous magnetic moment with incorporated hadronic contributions. Emergence is a key concept in complex system research, particularly when exploring the interplay between component properties and higher-level behavior. In the context of machine learning, numerous studies have applied complexity reduction and abstraction techniques to identify emergent properties. However, existing approaches primarily focus on detecting embodiment, which is typically defined as an internal representation of external information. Embodiment is readily identifiable in systems that interact with their environment through senses and actions. However, it is unclear whether embodiment can be confidently attributed to external agents, such as code repositories. To address this uncertainty, we propose a novel framework for studying embodiment in data collections and demonstrate its applicability to the co-evolution of source code and software repositories. Our findings indicate that large software repositories exhibit universal embodiment, with the collective structure of patches indicating a shared understanding among developers. This work presents a new direction for researching embodiment outside of traditional embodied systems. Additionally, it provides valuable insights into the collective knowledge and cognitive processes of the entire GitHub community. Although the embodiment approach has primarily been applied to biological and robotic systems, its extended scope is exemplified by recent studies on the embodiment of social systems and linguistic structures. Recently, there have also been emerging attempts to understand the embodiment of software and digital systems. Notably, digital embodiment is an emerging field that is likely to develop significant implications for the design and evolution of digital systems, with far-reaching consequences for the digital landscape. In this study, we have embarked on an empirical investigation of the embodiment of software repositories, with particular attention to the GitHub open-source platform. By examining the embedding of contributors and clients within the repository structure, we reveal a shared understanding and context among the community. This identification is then used to create a reliable index that tracks variations in vocal pitch over time. Since establishing a voice detection system that is fully autonomous in a real-world setting is extremely difficult due to issues like noise and signal quality variability, the proposed method focuses solely on voiced segments of speech. By employing a specific Kalman filter model adapted to both forward and backward tracking, the proposed algorithm is capable of accurately identifying voiced segments and calculating pitch values. These results are then analyzed and presented in a way that facilitates easy interpretation and use in a voice detection system. Testing was conducted on the TIMIT database and other practical signals, and the outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of this unsupervised algorithm. This algorithm is now being used in a voice detection system used to monitor the daily vocal activities of patients with laryngeal cancer. It has also been registered in the IEEE Signal Processing System Society as publication number #DCS_2022_52. In this study, we explore a scenario where IEEE 802.11.5 compatible devices, specifically cars, use millimeter wave frequencies to access broadband wireless services. The network architecture comprises fixed outdoor basestations and a moving cluster of vehicles. We are investigating a problem of channel allocation for an optimal distribution of bandwidth in these networks. A novel hybrid encoding approach is developed for an efficient frequency assignment mechanism. By combining the efficiency of continuous frequency allocation with the simplicity of discrete channel assignment, our hybrid encoding enables seamless integration of outdoor and in-vehicle client devices. Simulation results demonstrate the performance benefits of our hybrid encoding design. This research has been partially funded by ANI as part of a national project Number: 21ANI-076.

Federated Learning can facilitate collaborative AI training across multiple devices while maintaining users' data privacy. Yet, the current implementation of FL is only suitable for incremental model updates, which can lead to large data transfer requirements and prolonged training times. This study proposes a new testing framework to evaluate FL's efficiency in extracting pre-trained models from complex neural networks. The framework's early termination feature allows for the immediate assessment of models despite incomplete updates. Based on this framework, we discover that a small number of devices can efficiently contribute to FL's goal, and by selecting only these devices, we achieve significant reductions in communication cost without compromising performance. The proposed approach is demonstrated through various experiments involving different device configurations and network architectures. Specifically, we find that just one or two devices can efficiently contribute to FL's goal when extracting BERT-based models, and even with six-device configurations, the required iterations can be halved while maintaining comparable results. This streamlined process can provide valuable insights into model compression techniques and more effective federated extraction methods. The proposed framework is made available for reproduction of our study's results. The full code can be accessed at: https://github.com/jbarnesspain/FEEDBACK. This project is part of ARCO, an initiative that supports the development of trust-worthy AI systems in various domains, and is specifically related to ARCO's work on data privacy and Federated Learning, as depicted in this study. The proposed testing framework and resulting tools can support the development of FL-based systems in different settings, and may be particularly useful for initiatives like ARCO, which aims to promote the adoption of FL-based solutions in practice. Using density functional theory calculations with reliable approximations, a new family of promising topological insulators MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Cd, Hg) with notable energy gaps has been discovered. This discovery was facilitated by a systematic exploration of the Te-Tl-Cd (and Hg) phase diagram. Notably, these compounds exhibit robust mechanical stability, with the most stable configurations occurring in the P21/m and Pn21/a space groups. Through comprehensive analysis, it is established that MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Cd, Hg) exhibit characteristics of strong topological insulators due to the presence of a Z$_2$ inversion symmetry violation, coupled with an unusual occurrence of band inversion in Te, which contributes to their remarkable energy gaps. This is further validated by peculiar anisotropy in Fermi surface geometry, alongside an abundance of surface Dirac and Weyl states across various k-point paths, thus confirming the presence of protected Fermi arcs on the vortex surface. This is accompanied by an extensive theoretical investigation of the electronic and spin-anisotropic Hall effect in MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Cd, Hg) and their potential experimental indicators have been identified. Finally, it is hypothesized that MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Cd, Hg) can be successfully synthesized through melting, with the suggestion of using Te-rich conditions to enhance crystal quality. This is further reinforced by a binary phase diagram analysis between CdTe and TlTe, which indicates a highly stable area for CdTl$_4$Te$_3$ and suggests that MTl$_4$Te$_3$ (M = Hg) may also be obtained through liquid synthesis with modifications. Additionally, it is proposed that HgTl$_4$Te$_3$ can be obtained through a thermal decomposition reaction between HgTe and Tl$_2$Te. But what if we're seeking multiple optimal settings to different parameters? Traditional methods using utility functions can achieve this, but they come with a significant challenge: creating a customized utility function for each unique goal in our simulation study. This not only demands extensive expertise but also makes it difficult to adapt to changing goal sets or updated scientific understanding, as refining the function becomes nearly impossible. To overcome these limitations, we've developed a novel utility function-based approach that makes it possible to discover multiple optimal settings for diverse simulation outcomes with minimal expertise and a limited number of trials. This approach also enables easy integration of external insights into the simulation framework and efficiently adapts to changes in both the simulation parameters and the desired outcomes. Reinforcement learning agents can be vulnerable in certain situations. An opponent with partial knowledge of the environment can exploit this information to affect the learning process, even without knowing the agent's actions. This can be particularly challenging in reinforcement learning because agents may rely on hidden environmental factors or the opponent might provide outdated information. Existing research into "blackbox assaults" has focused on scenarios where an opponent has complete knowledge of the environment and can see the agent's actions. To address a gap in knowledge, we explore a more difficult scenario where an opponent has limited knowledge of the environment and our study finds that an opponent with partial knowledge can still affect the agent's decision-making process. Specifically, we discovered that an opponent can influence a reinforcement learning agent by as much as 80% when the agent uses unsupervised linear-temporal models with expected loss and that this influence can reach 40% with models that use supervised linear-temporal models with minimal assumptions. Additionally, we found that an opponent can significantly impact a reinforcement learning agent's performance in classic GridWorld and MabiMall environments, even when the agent uses sophisticated temporal models and adversarial training. Our research shows that it is possible to mount an assault on reinforcement learning agents without knowing their actions or getting direct feedback from them. In risk-aware reinforcement learning, policymakers balance obtaining rewards with limiting entropy, and research has primarily focused on modeling changes in reward systems using stationary linear models. Nevertheless, in many real-world situations, the linear model's reward system is not steady and cannot be assumed to be stable. Therefore, linear models are inadequate, and the current approach is unsuitable, resulting in a suboptimal policy. To address this issue, we introduce a non-constant variance reinforcement learning approach with adaptive recognition and separation. Using data-only, we develop a dynamic verification technique that detects changes in the reward system and adapts to non-stationary linear models. We design a new separator that minimizes entropy while taking into account both system variables and observation noise, and our theory guarantees that the resulting estimator reaches the minimum entropy without requiring any parameters. Moreover, our method achieves an optimal rate of convergence without any smoothness assumptions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and real-world applications, and our findings show that our method performs better than existing approaches, and the effectiveness of our separation design is confirmed through experiments. Additionally, our technique is versatile and can be applied to various non-constant variance situations. Overall, our work provides a groundbreaking solution to risk-aware reinforcement learning in non-stationary settings, and our code is publicly available.

We study the masterfields that emerge in the Bessel soliton family for the Ablowitz-Ladik equation when collision parameters $\mu$ and $\nu$ are equally divided among four values that form a symmetric set around zero. These solutions lead to solitons, antisolitons, and breathers, depending on the ring solution's sign and Bessel equation zero intersection patterns. Notably, this method allows for constructing two Tangible solutions, a $C^1$ solution and a $C^2$ solution, whose associated Lagrangians only differ by a constant. We demonstrate that our technique can accurately determine the Tangible solution, resolving issues with earlier approaches that might yield multiple results or no solutions. We also investigate how the Lagrangian of the $C^2$ solution is related to its motion equations, providing insights into its dynamics from its Hamiltonian form. Our study offers a simple approach to identifying planar soliton solutions, and it may be extended to more complex soliton families. Additionally, our findings reveal a surprising connection between the soliton equation's Hamiltonian form and the motion equations of its Tangible solution, shedding new light on their interdependence. We further demonstrate that for the Ablowitz-Ladik equation, the soliton equation's Hamiltonian is not only conserved but also connects the constant Lagrangians of the two Tangible solutions, effectively making them equivalent variants of a single solution when considered in relation to the equation's physical space, despite their differing forms in phase space. Our analysis provides new perspectives on solving the equation numerically and recovering its motion equations from a Hamiltonian form. Our analysis also validates the cooperation mechanism's efficacy in improving user aspect preferences and item exposure. We develop a novel framework to incorporate human feedback in reinforcement learning when some aspects of an agent's behavior are already optimized for a desired goal. Traditional inverse reinforcement learning assumes an environment and reward functions are unknown and unstructured; our approach builds upon these assumptions, introducing a hierarchical Bayesian model that learns these parameters in a learning-to-learn framework. The framework enables efficient learning of both reward functions and policy adaptations using only a few human demonstrations. The empirical evaluation on multiple simple gridworld domains demonstrates the proposed method's superiority over existing techniques under varying degrees of environmental uncertainty and human feedback availability. The hierarchical structure allows for the detection of common patterns across different tasks, resulting in better sample efficiency and a more stable policy discovery when compared to a method that learns independent reward functions for each task. Additionally, the empirical results show that our approach remains effective when some aspects of an agent's behavior are already optimized for a desired goal. The developed framework is a potential asset for reducing the cost and inefficiencies associated with inverse reinforcement learning in practical applications. In a typical scientific process, researchers start by studying relevant literature, formulating a hypothesis, conducting experiments, analyzing data, drawing conclusions, and finalizing their findings in an academic paper. This proven sequence was the standard procedure even a few decades ago, when scientists primarily relied on physical laboratories for experimental work. However, the significant advancement in digital technology has transformed the landscape of scientific research, largely shifting the experimental segment to the quiet hours of the night when computers tirelessly process data, render images, simulate real-world scenarios, and explore digital universes. While data analysis used to be a time-consuming part of the scientific process, it is now largely automated with the aid of advanced algorithms. Consequently, the extended collaboration with artificial intelligence has reduced the time required for finding patterns in complex data. Moreover, AI-driven tools have made possible the creation of virtual realities for studying complex systems without the need for physical resources. Despite these breakthroughs, the traditional sequence of the scientific research still adheres to the conventional approach of presenting AI-generated results as if they were produced by human intelligence. This reveals a significant gap in integrating the significant contributions of AI, whose unparalleled capabilities have become an essential part of the modern scientific workflow. This thesis aims to address the above-mentioned shortcomings, and in a series of experiments designed to examine the impact of AI, this study demonstrates the benefits of acknowledging the formidable capabilities of artificial intelligence in scientific research. With an eye on future developments, this research investigates how the increasing integration of AI will shape the next generation of scientists, engineers, and researchers, who are increasingly relying on machine intelligence to drive their work. Unlike traditional physical laboratories where researchers work in a well-organized environment to verify hypotheses, the extensive use of AI in recent years has led to a more dynamic and collaborative research environment, where next-generation researchers are leveraging the collective capabilities of artificial intelligence to accelerate the research process. This collaborative approach, where humans and machines work in harmony, is a significant departure from the traditional scientific methodology that once relied on human intelligence and effort. This study serves as a laboratory journal that documents our immersive experience in this exciting research environment, where artificial intelligence has become an integral part of the scientific research process. We hope that this digital journal will inspire future generations of scientists, engineers, and researchers to prioritize the significant contributions of artificial intelligence in driving scientific research and accelerating innovation. This digital journal is dedicated to exploring the next generation of collaborative research opportunities enabled by artificial intelligence. In recent years, graph neural networks have gained significant attention for data analysis, particularly in handling complex and partially observable relationships between data points. This interest can be attributed to their ability to leverage underlying latent patterns, facilitated by chance processes, that may underlie data. However, current graph neural networks rely on predetermined network structures, which are often ill-equipped to capture the inherent probabilistic nature of these patterns. To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel approach where the latent probability matrices that govern the relationships between data points are learned in a probabilistic framework. We develop two distinct methods, one based on a probabilistic differential equation and another based on a probabilistic graph, to tackle this learning problem. These methods enable the recovery of underlying chance graphs and can be applied to both generative and non-generative models, providing a deeper understanding of the probabilistic patterns that underlie the data. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach using various real-world datasets and find that our methods achieve state-of-the-art results, providing a more nuanced understanding of the data compared to existing approaches. The proposed methods also demonstrate superior interpretability in terms of their probabilistic groupings and latent probability dynamics. Furthermore, our methods are equally effective or even preferential in high-noise scenarios. The techniques we have developed are made available through our open-source Python 3 package called pyognn. With its pyognn module, users can now easily construct chance graphs from data, significantly simplifying the process. We also demonstrate the applicability of our methods in downstream tasks such as multi-way clustering and multi-modal data analysis. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the designed modules in our code, ensuring the reproducibility of our methods. The proposed methods were evaluated and found to be effective in a range of applications, extending their utility beyond their initial scope. The code for these methods is openly available at https://github.com/huutiany/pyognn. The datasets used in this research can be found at https://github.com/huutiany/pyognn/tree/master/data. The Python 3 package pyognn was utilized to implement the designed methods. We also openly share our code, which reproduces the key results, for thorough evaluation at https://github.com/huutiany/pyognn. To test the generalizability of our approach, we evaluated our methods on various real-world datasets and compared their performance to established benchmarks. We found that our methods achieved superior results, providing a more detailed understanding of the data and its probabilistic patterns

We begin by proving a theorem regarding Slim Sidon sequences, which demonstrates that if $\phi$ is a vectorial Boolean function with a non-trivial automorphism $\psi$ and a period of $n$, and if $\psi$ has order $m < n$, then the lowest degree of a Slim Sidon sequence for $\phi$ is at least $m$. We subsequently show that our result is applicable to several specific cases, such as $M_{13, 13}(x)$ and $M_{27, 3}(x)$. Furthermore, our work leads to a lower bound for the nonlinearity of a particular class of vectorial Boolean functions known as $NN$-functions. Specifically, for any $n$-variable $NN$-function $\phi$ with a period of $n$ and a non-trivial automorphism $\psi$ of order $m < n$, we find that the nonlinearity of $\phi$ is minimised when it is a permutation and we show that in such a case, the lowest degree of a Slim Sidon sequence for $\phi$ is at least $m$. Furthermore, for any $n$-variable $NN$-function $\phi$ with a period of $n$ and a non-trivial automorphism $\psi$ of order $m < n$, we find that the nonlinearity of $\phi$ is minimised when it is a permutation and we show that in such a case, the lowest degree of a Slim Sidon sequence for $\phi$ is at least $m$. We establish the existence of stochastic subgroups within acylindrically hyperbolic groups, which exhibit loyal and invariant characteristics. The notion of stochastic subgroups was initially introduced by Clade in groups exhibiting non-elastic behavior. The proof of this current finding relies heavily on Clade's proof, along with an additional analysis involving quasi-isometries and the properties of acylindrical hyperbolicity. The result can be applied to certain types of groups, such as free-by-circuits groups, and it is proven that the stochastic subgroups derived from these groups are inherently nonfinite. This discovery also yields a novel demonstration of nonfiniteness for groups exhibiting certain stochastic characteristics, thereby providing a generalized version of a previous finding by Kapovich and Weidman. The study of stochastic subgroups may offer insights into understanding whether groups exhibiting certain stochastic characteristics are inherently infinite. The existence of these subgroups within acylindrically hyperbolic groups also suggests the possibility of existing parallels between the theories of non-elastic and acylindrical hyperbolicity. The research provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to identify nonfinite properties in various groups. Two fundamental types of spatial representations - metric and topological - underlie our understanding of space. Although both concepts are theoretically significant, their practical applications vary in terms of predictivity and scope for modification. This chapter illustrates how the principle of reinforcement learning in artificial intelligence can inform the development of biologically inspired spatial representations. Particularly, it demonstrates how selecting suitable tasks and leveraging inherent biases in both neural networks and the environment can facilitate the emergence of metric spatial representations from scratch. Additionally, the chapter discusses the implications of these findings for biologically inspired spatial representations, emphasizing the need to consider the interplay between environmental constraints and learned mappings. This perspective could lead to new insights into the underlying mechanisms of spatial cognition in biology. Moreover, the lessons learned from reinforcement learning can promote a more proactive approach in the study of spatial cognition, shifting from solely explanatory to actively manipulating and modifying spatial representations as well as their underlying neural substrates. Finally, the chapter concludes by highlighting potential applications and ethical implications of which genetic spatial modifications could lead to a 'geometric theory' of spatial cognition. 

Keywords: spatial representations, reinforcement learning, artificial and biological applications, metric and topological space, deep learning and neural networks, intrinsic and extrinsic biases in environments and neural networks, predictive accuracy and modification, geometric theory of spatial cognition, cognitive engineering and design.

The recent advancement of deep neural networks has brought about significant enhancements in the recognition of sound events. This paper presents an innovative method for accurately localizing and identifying sound events in an audio clip. We utilize a linear convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, incorporating rectangular filters to process long, non-adjacent signal segments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this filter shape through comparative analysis with standard temporal filter shapes. Additionally, we introduce an optimized data augmentation technique for the sound event detection task by incorporating channel rotation into existing methods. A comprehensive database of 3260 sound event clips from 20 categories and 5 environmental backgrounds is employed to train and evaluate our model and competing frameworks. Our experimental results show that our proposed model achieves a wide range of accuracy across multiple metrics: mean accuracy across all scenes increases by 4.13%, metric over all scenes increases by 11.69%, and mean F1-score across all scenes increases by 6.35%. Our model surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance reported on the DCASE 2020 task by a considerable margin. A thorough investigation of hyperparameter influence is carried out, revealing the optimal filter shape and channel rotation parameters for our model. Our method is made accessible through an open-source implementation. The approach involves translating these restrictions into logical expressions and using them to develop consistency and feasibility conditions. Unlike traditional case models, where object occurrence is binary (either present or absent), cardinality restrictions introduce a spectrum of possible occurrences. Consistency is assessed by ensuring predicted outcomes align with specified restrictions, whereas feasibility is determined by considering the minimum number of objects needed to satisfy a given scenario. A practical example illustrates the application of these concepts in modeling. Unlike existing tools, which often require manually defining feasibility sets, this approach automates the process by leveraging a system that generates all potential object combinations and then filters them in accordance with specified constraints. Wildfires disrupting solar radiation with hazardous air quality effects have become more frequent in recent years, especially in the Western United States. Understanding the behavior of wildfires is therefore crucial for predicting aerosol levels and maintaining air quality standards. By analyzing satellite data from multiple sources, a machine learning-based approach is developed to forecast aerosol levels using physics-based principles. This is achieved by incorporating inverse problems to estimate key parameters affecting aerosol production, such as fire intensity and atmospheric conditions. By optimizing these parameters, the model is able to accurately replicate observed aerosol measurements, achieving a notable 15% enhancement in prediction accuracy. By integrating this system with climate modeling and data assimilation techniques, the overall air quality modeling framework exhibits promising capabilities. An individual's location is considered private when the relationship between their current location and previous locations does not reveal any identifiable information. We use conditional expectations to define and study this concept of location privacy. Our investigation involves examining location privacy with two specific metrics: the maximum amount of identifiable information and the minimum amount of identifiable information within a privacy boundary. We demonstrate that determining the minimum amount of identifiable information is a more complex problem than finding the maximum amount, but demonstrate a method for simplifying this investigation under specific circumstances. We also explore how to optimize a system's privacy settings by balancing privacy and performance in a location tracking model. Our investigation includes a numerical study utilizing synthetic data as well as an analysis of a well-known dataset, revealing that our proposed method yields better results and reduced computational costs compared to other approaches. Our research provides a framework for assessing location privacy using conditional expectations, enabling more accurate evaluations and improved systems with better balance between privacy and performance. Our approach can be adapted for use with other monitoring systems, such as surveillance cameras, by considering the relationships between locations and identifying information under specific conditions. Additionally, our framework may be expanded to account for other factors that affect privacy, such as data sensitivity and detection probabilities. We also hypothesize that our method could be useful in real-world applications involving location-based services, such as delivering targeted advertisements based on an individual's known locations. Our research may lead to contributions in these areas, such as reducing privacy breaches and supporting privacy-conscious users by enabling them to make informed decisions about their location privacy. Our investigation also reveals potential avenues for future research, such as employing machine learning techniques to model the relationships between locations and identifying information, well beyond our current study. Our framework relies on specific assumptions regarding these relationships, but we anticipate that future studies will lead to more sophisticated models utilizing machine learning. Our numerical study demonstrates how to utilize synthetic data and the widely-used Taxicab dataset in our investigation, but we expect that future research will involve a broader range of datasets, such as the Geolocation dataset. Our approach in changing privacy settings while maintaining performance may lead to future developments in location-based software development, such as increasing the built-in privacy settings in a user's device while ensuring comparable service quality. Our study, and future research, may contribute to reducing identifiable information when an individual's location is shared. Fisher's contributions to genetics emphasize his opposition to Mendelian genetics due to perceived inaccuracies in Mendel's calculations, suggesting he preferred a polygenic model over single-gene inheritance. However, this perspective disproportionately reflects Fisher's longstanding disagreements with the scientific community, primarily stemming from his causal theory of population genetics, as evidenced by his 1930 book "The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection." This view is also influenced by a misunderstanding of Fisher's proposed mean nonadditive genetic influence and its significance in his causal theory. We reexamine the rationale behind Fisher's theory and demonstrate that his approach is a legitimate contribution to genetics, as well as an extension of his earlier statistical work, including his 1914 research on the infinitely infinite multivariate population. Notably, recent statistical analyses, such as Buckwalter's 2008 work, have found that mean nonadditive genetic influences are relatively small, supporting Fisher's later views on the importance of studying the distribution of traits in relation to selection and gene frequency changes. We argue that Buckwalter's findings, combined with the limited impact of Fisher's views on modern genetics, result in part from the isolation of Fisher's work in the fields of genetics and evolutionary biology. We aim to overcome this isolation by highlighting the causal significance of Fisher's mean impact and its potential contributions to current research in biostatistics and econometrics, as well as his influence on the work of Neyman and Pearl. Furthermore, we contend that a more in-depth analysis of Fisher's contributions is necessary to assess his actual influence on the development of modern genetics. To this end, we propose constructing an index of long-term influence for measuring the enduring impact of significant scientific publications. We conduct an exhaustive decomposition of the complete Hamiltonian into its uniquely defined components, thereby establishing a comprehensive framework for studying the pair Hamiltonian of this mixture. Within this framework, we identify the fundamental coupling parameters, establish their physical meanings, and demonstrate the pairwise nature of the Hamiltonian's spectrum. Furthermore, we prove that the low-lying multiplet structure is universally encoded across various representations and show that the nature of excited states is exclusively determined by the relative weights of different couplings. Our findings are verified through both numerical simulations and experimental data analysis. Consequently, the reduced pair Hamiltonian model, parameterized by two distinct coupling strengths, effectively describes the pairwise interactions within the system. Based on this outcome, we propose a concrete strategy for conducting in-depth pair interaction measurements in cold atom experiments, thereby significantly enhancing our understanding of the system's physics. Ultimately, the present approach is adaptable to more complex mixtures of fermions and can be applied to various contexts, such as QCD physics, as exemplified by the mixing of proton and neutron. Preoperative planning in surgical procedures such as weight loss surgery, relies heavily on computed tomography (CT) scans which can be substituted by low-dose X-ray (LDX) images taken during the procedure. However, LDX images are compromised by noise which hinders accurate tissue and organ identification, including smoke signals used for surgical quality assessment. Recent studies have explored noise reduction techniques, primarily evaluated on an industrial dataset. This study examines if noise reduction and image enhancement methods can be effective in real-world laparoscopic surgery settings by leveraging the FastGAN-based method mentioned in a previous study. Our analysis indicates that noise reduction and image enhancement can significantly impact smoke signal detection, suggesting that data-driven methods may benefit from such processing. Interestingly, we found that introducing smoke signals into the FastGAN method leads to better performance and increased 'average' scores in organ segmentation, particularly for the smoke signal. Notably, we observed that the FastGAN method can accurately identify smoke signals, organs, and tissues without ground truth, highlighting its potential for automatic smoke signal detection. Our analysis also suggests that the FastGAN method may be adapted for smoke signal detection by adjusting the loss function. This study presents new findings and suggests future research directions for automatic smoke signal detection using deep learning models. The code and additional information are publicly available. Mobile devices are susceptible to attacks launched by malicious access points (APs) that infiltrate their systems via the radio signal exchange. Defenses put in place to shield these devices are inadequate and often vulnerable to manipulation, allowing the devices to remain exposed to attacks. A powerful strategy for countering such threats is evident in passive defense mechanisms, specifically the Plan Based Adaptive (PBA) technique, which offers excellent protection. The PBA technique is renowned for its proactive measures, identifying and eliminating hazardous signals in real-time, effectively neutralizing attacks. Although the PBA technique is highly effective, it is subject to two significant limitations. First, it solely considers the temporal characteristics of signals in making decisions, thus not fully utilizing available information. Second, we have identified a pattern in which attacks occasionally transition into prolonged periods of inactivity, thereby decreasing the likelihood of being detected. To address these shortfalls, we present an enhanced method, referred to as the CT-PBA (Communication Transfer Based PBA) technique. The CT-PBA technique bridges the gap by introducing a novel decision making process that incorporates both temporal and spatial characteristics of signals. Additionally, it closes the gap by identifying a signal pattern that predicts prolonged periods of inactivity, thereby detecting inactive signals that may hide attacks. The effectiveness of the CT-PBA technique is showcased through simulation and practical experiments, which demonstrate that it surpasses the PBA technique in accuracy and false positive rate performance. The experimental findings confirm that the CT-PBA technique achieves a notable decrease in detection delay and a notable increase in detection accuracy, specifically a 91.52% improvement in localization and 75.76% in tracking. Furthermore, it yields the most minimal average path distance among all competitors. The code for this research is openly accessible at the link provided. Additionally, we have obtained patent documentation for this work. In conclusion, the CT-PBA technique represents an adaptive and resilient solution to detect and prevent attacks in radio-based localization and tracking systems, particularly in situations involving multiple and intelligent threats. The method's exceptional performance and relatively simple implementation make it an ideal choice for both academic researchers and industry professionals. Specifically, it addresses the challenge of detecting attacks that may portend prolonged periods of inactivity. Furthermore, it offers an effective strategy to surpass the limitations of solely considering temporal characteristics in decision making. In addition, it introduces a communication pattern that reveals an attack's progression into a prolonged period of inactivity. The proposed method has been thoroughly evaluated through both theoretical and experimental approaches, demonstrating its superiority over the current best techniques.

The Cotton tensor, a four-dimensional, antisymmetric tensor derived from the Riemann tensor, shares close ties with the source-free gravitational field equations in four dimensions. When expressed in a coordinate system with vanishing Cotton tensor, the Riemann tensor remains constant over time, implying that appearance of the Cotton tensor is a crucial indicator of dynamic gravitational fields. Furthermore, the Cotton tensor offers a mathematically robust approach to derive the equations that describe how mass and angular momentum are conserved in general relativity. By utilizing this approach, we demonstrate that the conventional definition of mass and angular momentum, derived from the Poincaré-Cartan symplectic structure, remains conserved in the presence of gravitational fields derived from a general metric. Additionally, this method reveals that gravitational energy is indeed defined uniquely up to a Poincaré transformation. Researchers have introduced an innovative technique for accurately measuring masses of short-lived, unusual nuclei that exist for less than a second. This method utilizes the $B\rho$-defined isochronous mass spectrometry technique, which was successfully implemented at the SHICAD electron beam ion trap at Lanzhou, China. Although initially used to study nuclei with positive charges, the technique has been modified to aid in the mass measurement of nuclei with negative charges. The modifications involved using a magnetic electric particle trap at the RIKEN Nishina Center in Japan to demonstrate the feasibility of measuring masses for low-mass, short-lived nuclei in a different setup. This breakthrough could help researchers better understand nuclei's internal structure. Parameters from the experiment at RIKEN, such as the mass defect, were compared with theoretical predictions and found to be significantly more accurate than previous estimates, with an average margin of error as low as 290 kiloelectronvolts per atomic mass unit. These precise measurements have significantly narrowed the gap between current nuclear physics research and the predictions of theoretical models. Most importantly, the research has provided valuable, precise data that will serve as a foundation for future measurements and may aid in refining the preliminary data in the mass table's initial report. Recent advancements in Automated Machine Learning have yielded a technique, 
Standardizing Flows, which can be applied across diverse fields and has 
exhibited promising results in lattice field theory. This tutorial is tailored 
for researchers familiar with lattice field theories but lacking expertise in 
machine learning, as it presents an alternative method to address mapping 
problems using only elementary machine learning concepts. We demonstrate how 
Standardizing Flows can be utilized to solve key challenges in lattice field 
theory, such as mapping and thermodynamic calculations, also outlining its 
connection to determinant methods. Additionally, we will discuss how this 
approach can be extended to explore topological properties in lattice field 
theory. This tutorial is an adaptation of a original BAYES 2022 lecture and 
is intended to introduce and familiarize researchers with the application of 
Standardizing Flows in lattice field theory.

Top quarks can be identified through their decay channels into leptons or jets, but the resulting signals are typically masked by background noise. The primary goal of this research is to develop an algorithm that can differentiate between genuine top quark signals and artificial noise, specifically through examining the characteristics of top quark and jet formations in proton-lead collisions. By analyzing these features, the research can determine the top-quark lead-jet mass and compare it to the predicted values, ultimately confirming the top quark's existence. The study utilizes a statistical approach called Bayesian inference to validate the top-quark generation in proton-lead collisions. The resulting findings support the presence of top quarks with masses ranging from 290 to 630 GeV/c^2, consistent with the predicted values. The research also serves as a benchmark for confirming generation levels in future experiments, particularly those analyzing more precise data from the Large Hadron Collider. The research can significantly contribute to understanding top quark properties and how it interacts with matter, particularly in high-energy collisions. Developing a text-to-SQL parsing system that comprehends the semantics of database queries is a complex challenge. Most existing systems rely on large annotated datasets, but acquiring sufficient, accurate annotations is impractical due to the time-consuming nature of annotation. Additionally, systems trained on incomplete annotations struggle to grasp semantic meanings, limiting their effectiveness. To tackle this problem, we've formulated a new paradigm for cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, incorporating an auxiliary task that generates human-readable instructions for data annotation. This auxiliary task not only aids in learning but also provides valuable annotations. We've designed a full pipeline to leverage annotated data from other domains through automatic translation and employ transfer learning and data augmentation to enhance our parser's performance. Our method has achieved superior results on the real-world banki dataset, surpassing the performance of current state-of-the-art systems both in terms of execution efficiency and accuracy. Notably, our method has also produced a large annotated dataset, providing a useful resource for future research. The code and dataset can be accessed through https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-Vision/tree/main/dbql.

This paper introduces an innovative "multigoal-oriented mistake correction strategy," which adjusts model parameters to match experimental data while considering multiple variables, in the context of heated substance processing. The technique demonstrates its ability to correct model errors for both single and double heat transfer scenarios using the generalized Boussinesq model. Analysis of the corrections made to the Prandtl number reveals that local heat transfer experiments primarily correct the model's conductive component, whereas global studies also correct the convective component. Furthermore, a proposed metric assesses the model's accuracy against experimental heat flux and temperature data, providing a more comprehensive understanding of model performance. The research shows that adjusting the Prandtl number has a significant impact on the model's convective heat transfer calculations. Although the proposed method generates physically plausible corrections, further work is needed to establish its connection to physical properties. The study highlights the potential of the multigoal mistake correction strategy for identifying and modifying imperfect model assumptions. The research was conducted using numerical simulations and is available as an open-source package, named OpenMOC,NC. The development aims to facilitate the efficient utilization of numerical models by correcting any discrepancies between simulation results and actual data, thereby increasing their accuracy and reliability. Future work will focus on generalizing the method across various model types and identifying the physical implications of the proposed correction approach. The code is publicly accessible at the following link: https://github.com/NUMA-NUME/MOCNC/tree/mccstrategy, with the reference URL: https://nume.numec.org.br/nume/numerical-methods/publications/2022/multigoal-oriented-mist-correction-strategy.ashx.

We investigate reduction techniques and associated time complexities for a category of stacking problems encompassing well-known ABP-counting challenges, aiming to establish kernelization procedures with predictable runtime for these problems. This involves defining a parameterized reduction process that maintains a reduced input size dependent on the parameter value. While kernelization may not be feasible for many counting problems, we demonstrate the possibility of obtaining a linearly reduced kernel for certain special cases with fixed-parameter solutions. This reduces input size to a function of the parameter value p, with a constant or logarithmic dependency on p. This research completely solves the ABP-counting problems for multiset partition lattice and provides LP solutions for the multiset partition enumeration and alliance partition problems. This progress indicates that kernelization may be feasible for counting problems with algebraic structures as long as they have a finite and soluble lattice. In various contexts, such as social networks and financial relationships, it is commonly observed that individuals or entities tend to establish connections with others sharing similar characteristics or those anticipated to offer benefits. Building on this concept of preferential attachment, we investigate how interactions among entities involving multiple aspects can lead to the co-evolution of their relationships and characteristics. Our study focuses on a structural equilibrium model where agents' interactions result in mutual benefits, and it is demonstrated that views, representing the underlying connections, are inherently linked to the network topology, resulting in the amplification of existing associations and the formation of new connections among similar entities. Our analysis also reveals that, in the absence of a comprehensive network view, agents may settle into localized equilibrium states within their immediate surroundings, and these states may not accurately represent the overall network dynamics. It is further shown that third parties can facilitate assurance by facilitating face-to-face interactions between entities sharing similar characteristics and by mitigating risks associated with unexpected encounters between entities with little in common. Ultimately, our findings provide insights into the interconnected nature of structural equilibrium models and the distribution of views, and highlight the significance of trust in facilitating relationships among entities with little in common. Furthermore, our analysis sheds light on the relationship between views and networks, revealing that views can lead to the concentration of assets among a select few (the 'rich getting richer'), and demonstrates the role of assurance in disrupting this dynamic. Our research offers a novel perspective on the underlying mechanisms of trust and its relationship with the structural equilibrium models commonly used to understand social and economic interactions. Specifically, we examine how trust may lead to the misallocation of resources and assets, particularly when certain individuals or groups have access to information about each other's characteristics, effectively creating a divide in terms of relationships and interactions. Our findings provide a framework for understanding the distribution of assets and relationships, and the role of trust in shaping these dynamics, and ultimately highlight the need to adopt a broad perspective when analyzing interactions and exchanges within social and economic networks. By studying green star equations with a nearly constant effective speed, we found the fuzzy black hole's interior, including a region where the local density is concentrated. Additionally, we determined that the overall mass of this asymptotically level fuzzy black hole is no more than half the mass of a standard black hole with the same event horizon. We also calculated that when a star collapses into this type of black hole, more than 70% of its original mass is retained within the new, asymptotically level fuzzy black hole. Furthermore, we determined that these structures can form from a specific type of collapsed star with masses ranging from approximately 0.26 to 1.00 solar masses, primarily featuring hydrogen and/heavy elements in their composition. Within the range of radii 1.15 to 1.85 solar radii (for a 1 solar mass star), we found the most suitable progenitor candidates for these asymptotically level fuzzy black holes. We also explored other physical characteristics of these structures, including their electrical charge, event horizon, and size, particularly in relation to ultracompact white dwarfs, standard black holes, and black holes with reflective surfaces. These aspects lead us to speculate about various phenomena related to level-fuzzy black holes, including their potential connection to the 'Faint Faint Faint' phenomenon observed in 2020 and the radio counterparts of the events GW190814 and GW190521. We concluded by highlighting the potential links between level-fuzzy black holes and a broad range of observed phenomena, as well as their broader implications. We propose calling these structures 'asymptotically level fuzzy black stars' (ALFBSs) to describe their unique properties. We further studied the possibility of core-collapse supernovae forming ALFBSs, including cases involving neutron star mergers and other related events. This research examines well-posedness for a broad class of hyperbolic Cauchy problems with coefficients that have sublogarithmic growth and smooth initial data. We show that for any given sublogarithmic rate, the associated initial value problem has a universally defined, continuous solution within a corresponding time frame. Additionally, we demonstrate that this result reaches its theoretical limit for coefficients growing at a logarithmic rate and that smooth data require time growth restrictions for the well-posedness theorem to apply. We prove this category of well-posedness through a combination of methods including energy estimates, Lebesgue space manipulations, and the Friedrichs' commutator estimate in modified forms. This study expands on prior work by Chaudret, Hani, and Varoquoye who investigated similar topics but subjected solutions to time-Lp(n<2)-norms. In contrast, we employ time-L2-norms, allowing for the well-posedness theorem to be articulated in a straightforward manner. Furthermore, our research addresses well-posedness for a broad class of half-wave equations, providing a thorough understanding of the theorem's scope and illustrating the importance of coefficients' growth rates. We also discuss how our research and its underlying techniques empower the development of a microlocal approach to hyperbolic partial differential equations. This study is a fulfillment of research tasks under Professor Jean-Francois Peyerimhoff's guidance.

Medical researchers heavily rely on Sign Language notes to understand and analyze real-world medical scenarios. Despite the importance of these notes, they pose a challenge due to being written in a less common language and incorporating specialized terminology from the medical field. To tackle this issue, machine learning models are developed to automatically extract relevant information from these notes. However, these models primarily focus on adapting to distribution shifts within existing data or using domain-downsampled pretraining methods. To improve this, we introduce a novel approach called DomainGeneralize. This approach incorporates data augmentation and multiple-game non-stationary training that enables Sign Event Detection models to better navigate among diverse datasets of different sign language varieties. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, we created the Medical Sign Language (MSL) dataset, comprising medical notes written in two different languages, to simulate real-world domain generalization scenarios in Sign Language notes. Our results show that DomainGeneralize outperforms existing methods and performs nearly as well as training separate models per domain while generalizing the other domain. This document outlines the comprehensive approach of our Profound Team to tackle the Advanced Driving Challenge (ADC) 2021. Our proposal details how we intend to develop a sophisticated Artificial Intelligence (AI) system to navigate the ADC course. The course requirements necessitate a complex driving strategy that incorporates both short-term and long-term decision-making elements. Specifically, our solution focuses on implementing a Reinforcement Learning (RL) method utilizing Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to effectively tackle the ADC challenges. The core of our approach lies in its two-pronged strategy: Short-term planning will be achieved through an on-board policy function operating within an AD map, facilitated by Google's Colab platform and open-source software frameworks. Long-term planning will be enabled through an off-board historical database (long-term database) gathered from the short-term planning's experience, also known as the knowledge base. The off-board long-term planning agent (action planner) operates separately on a distant server and shares knowledge with the on-board agent (local policy function) via the network for shared information. The off-board agent uses deep RL techniques to generate short-term goals for the on-board agent based on the off-board agent's long-term planning insights. Similarly for the multi-agent aspect of our solution we used a separate off-board agent (the communicator) to develop a communication strategy between the off-board and on-board agents. This approach may seem complex but it simplifies the difficulty of developing an AI that can learn and improve over time by dividing the problem into smaller more manageable parts. Ultimately our solution harnesses the power of distributed computing and AI's ability to improve over time through reinforcement learning to develop an advanced driving strategy that can tackle the ADC's challenges efficiently and effectively.

This interest stems from TEEs' ability to provide robust security protections even in the presence of adversarial operations.
