In numerical relativity, implementing Hamiltonian and momentum preservation in the Time-Time-Kinematic formulation leads to a second-order accurate evolution system that handles gravitational waves and compact binary mergers effectively. This method has been successful in extending the lifespan of numerical simulations by one order of magnitude compared to standard techniques. Recent improvements have addressed the issues of constraint violation through the application of bison, a high-performance solver for nonlinear equations that takes advantage of advanced computer architecture. This breakthrough enables long-term simulations of binary black-hole mergers with precise control over the system's long-term properties. Specifically, we have achieved continuous observations of binary black-hole mergers from one day to one year in time, and performed numerous studies on post-merger phenomena during this extended period. These studies include accretion disk evolution, mass distribution of gold and platinium black holes, and various other research areas that were previously inaccessible to numerical relativity. To facilitate the efficiency of these extended simulations, we have developed a strategy to split computational workloads into different time spans, and assigned separate numerical schemes according to their properties. This method, called the History-Based Template Lemma, successfully increases the overall efficiency of numerical simulations by a significant factor. In particular, we have achieved a tenfold improvement in the overall efficiency of extended simulations by combining multiple contributons effectively. To verify the accuracy and robustness of TTK models, we have conducted a series of convergence tests that demonstrate second-order accurate evolution results for a variety of numerical models. Furthermore, we have achieved continuous coverage of gravitational wave spectra up to a frequency of 1 Hz in studies of binary black-hole mergers by implementing the improved methods mentioned above. To facilitate the application of TTK models in astrophysical simulations, we have developed a package called GIZMO-GW, which includes various built-in models for numerical relativity that can be used effectively. This package has been verified and used in a range of 1Hz GW-frequency studies, and has enabled significant advancements in the field, particularly through the development of prescribed-potential models that allow for more accurate simulations of galaxy clusters, disk galaxies, and other astronomical objects. To make the improved models more adaptable and efficient in numerical relativity, we have introduced a class of theoretical models called the TTK-theory, which provides a universal framework for developing Hamiltonian and momentum-preserving evolution systems. Specifically, we have proved that the theory's generic model satisfies the requirements of geodesic autoparallel sections, which in turn leads to the improved models mentioned above.

In recent years, a significant shift has occurred towards using deep learning techniques for time series forecasting. The primary challenge in employing deep learning for this purpose lies in the difficulty of automatically extracting relevant features from raw time series data. This problem can be further complicated by the presence of irregularly spaced data points, which require interpolation to facilitate modeling. Our proposed framework addresses this issue by utilizing a dynamic adaptation mechanism to identify the underlying features in multivariate time series data. The mechanism involves constructing a graph from the input data using a nearest neighbor approach, which is then modified to accommodate missing and noisy data by applying a soft attention technique. The resulting graph allows our adaptive graph convolutional network to extract relevant features through iterative applications of spatial and temporal convolutional operations. Experimental evaluations using various datasets reveal that our proposed model excels in terms of forecasting accuracy, particularly when compared to leading competing models, and also showcases its ability to adapt and generalize across different dataset scales. Recently, pre-trained models have achieved remarkable success in various education-related tasks. However, due to the high cost and scarcity of labeled data, particularly those taught by experienced instructors, universities struggle to establish reliable assessment methods. To address this challenge, our approach focuses on efficiently utilizing multi-instructor labeled data to maximize the performance of state-of-the-research models. Our method, Pairwise Iterative Logits Coalition (PILE), consists of two main components. First, it selectively updates multi-instructor logits based on the relationships between different instructors' confidence patterns. Building on this foundation, it iteratively adjusts the model's logits to match the distribution of high-quality human labels. Our experiments have demonstrated that our approach outperforms existing non-adaptive methods and achieves comparable performance to models trained on single-instructor datasets while performing 13% better than models trained on low-quality multi-instructor datasets. Ultimately, PILE has shown great potential in helping educational institutions overcome the challenges posed by diverse teaching staff and providing a solid foundation for future distillation methods. Our code and additional information can be found at https://github.com/melodyyzy/PILE. We have also established an online evaluation platform to demonstrate PILE's efficacy in real-time applications at https://edu-open.com/0.8/uncertainty/index.html. Key features of our approach include its universal applicability to various models, instructors, and datasets, as well as its ease of use: simply replace the model's logit's last layer with our pre-trained weights and adjust two hyperparameters to match the distribution of high-quality human labels. Additionally, our method has been adapted for use in non-labeled, few-shot learning scenarios where the model is presented with annotations from a single instructor under time constraints. Notably, our approach has shown great success in the education-related benchmark dataset, multiple choice question answering, where the model outperformed existing benchmarks by a significant 12.6% margin on human-labeled data and 11.3% on machine-labeled data. Our results have also highlighted the potential for models to exhibit biases based on various demographic and linguistic factors, as well as the complexity and quality of the learning material. Our study has provided a systematic analysis of these biases and their causes, demonstrating the feasibility of training models to overcome them. We suggest a novel method,'stimulated strength interferometry,' for detecting ultralight bosonic dark matter using short, intense laser pulses. The proposed technique involves utilizing the non-linear force between the dark matter particles and photons. As a bypass route to directly observing the dark matter's ultra-low momentum transfer, our method leverages the dark matter's unique interaction properties. Upon near-threshold energy absorption by the dark matter particles, the radiation pressure exerted on the ions rapidly amplifies the momentum transfer, enabling the identification of the dark matter particles through the resultant double-humped pattern in the probe ion's recoil distribution. Following the development of advanced tabletop facilities capable of generating intense, focused femtosecond laser pulses, our proposed technique seems feasible for the precise identification of the ultralight dark matter particles in the 10^-16 eV energy range. Furthermore, tabletop experiments using the proposed setup could potentially cover an extensive frequency range of 10^-16 to 10^-8 eV. In addition, the developed theoretical framework for strength interferometry provides a general paradigm for the microscopical understanding of the interaction between particles and fields, which has broader applications. This method also offers an original perspective on the paradigm of cross-platform and frequency-dependent cosmological dark matter detection. Last but not least, we use our findings to demonstrate that the frequency range of 10^-16 to 10^-14 eV is within reach of tabletop experiments, which could significantly verify the theory of wave-particle interaction over a vast frequency range of 10^-14 to 10^-9 eV. In conclusion, stimulated strength interferometry holds great potential for accurately understanding the phenomenon of wave-particle interaction and further validating the theory of dark matter. Network security systems rely heavily on compile-time decoders to ensure rapid,
high-fidelity system performance. The P416 match-action table format has gained
prominence due to its flexibility and efficiency in coding complex network policies.
This paper introduces an open-source P416 compiler framework that offers a versatile
approach to compiling P416 tables with various encoding methods, such as SPD and
Trie, for flexible network function orchestration. The compiler's modular design
and versatility in coding methods enable clear presentation and comparison of
different compilation strategies, including optimizations using high-order semantics.
The compiler's open-source nature allows for the community to share and compare
compilation codes, effectively moderating the search for the best compilation
approaches. Furthermore, we present novel improvements to SPD and Trie encoding
methods, along with an in-depth analysis that showcases our compiler's capacity
for clear presentation of different compilation strategies and their respective
performance differences. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy and
efficiency of our compiler and the substantial compilation and matching
performances gained through our optimized coding approaches. Specifically, the
compiler's default settings yields a 3.96X improvement in compilation scale and a
2.45X improvement in matching speed, while the compiler's best settings yields a
4.96X improvement in compilation scale and a 2.90X improvement in matching speed
over generic and hybrid approaches. Moreover, our compiler's capacity for precise
performance isolation and domain-specific optimization allows for enhanced
scalability, achieving a 10Gbps matching throughput on a single commodity CPU.

This method is theoretically validated and supported by additional numerical studies verifying its effectiveness. Consequently, the novel approach provides a reliable alternative for conveyance equation discretisations, particularly when dealing with complex geometries that are better suited to quadrilateral finite elements. A key goal of machine learning (ML) is to create accurate models that respect individuals' rights to privacy, particularly in the legal context of the United States. Traditional machine learning training techniques overlook the legal requirements of confidentiality, ignoring the fact that data can be imperfect and subject to litigation. However, with the emergence of decentralized federated learning (FL) methods, this oversight can be addressed. FL's regime of horizontal justice and differential privacy aligns with the legal standards of justice and confidentiality. Specifically, we connect the FL concept of justice to the legal principles of justice, and we relate the FL concept of differential privacy to the legal concept of confidentiality. We then discuss how the distinct meanings of justice and confidentiality interact within the FL framework and highlight open questions related to the legal interpretation of differential privacy. Ultimately, we explore how the values of justice and confidentiality dictate specific training techniques that balance accuracy with data protection, and we examine case studies illustrating the potential consequences of legal noncompliance in ML. Finally, we provide a future outlook on decentralized FL, emphasizing the need for further research in this area. Researchers have observed an excited state of the $B_c^+$ particle for the first time, using data collected by the LHCb experiment between 2015 and 2016, discovering two distinct states, one that decays into a proton and a $\Lambda_K^-$ and another into a proton and a $\Lambda\pi^-$, both decaying into a proton and a $\Xi_K^-$. The two states were found to have the same mass of around 6840 MeV but differ in their electrical charges. The observed states match predictions for the $B_c^+(2S1/2)$ state with a mass of 6840.2 MeV and a width of 1.6 meV, respectively. The discovery of the $B_c^+$ state in the proton and a $\Lambda\pi^-$ combination is slightly broader with a width of 3.3 meV. The study further revealed the branching fractions of the $B_c^+$ state decaying into a proton and a $\Lambda\pi^-$ or a $\LambdaK^-$, both at around 2% with a margin of error. The observation of the $B_c^+$ state decaying into a proton and a $\Lambda\pi^-$ is slightly broader with a margin of error. The study further revealed the $B_c^+$ meson's charge distribution and its structure, showing that the ratio of decays to a proton and a $\Lambda\pi^-$ or a $\LambdaK^-$ is around 0.83 with a margin of error. The study further revealed the decay pattern of the $B_c^+$ meson to a proton and a $\LambdaK^-$, showing that the ratio of the branching fraction to the standard model prediction is around 0.64 with a margin of error. The study further revealed the sensitivity of the decay pattern of the $B_c^+$ meson to the $B_c^+$ meson's structure and its properties. The discovery of the $B_c^+$ state decaying into a proton and a $\Lambda\pi^-$ or a $\LambdaK^-$ opens up new possibilities for future research on heavy mesons and their properties, particularly in understanding mesons composed of different quark combinations and their excited states. The study further revealed the potential for future discoveries using the LHCb experiment and its ability to advance our knowledge of heavy mesons and their properties. A recently introduced runge-kutta method called Continuous-Phase Runge-Kutta enjoys widespread applications in signal processing and information theory due to its flexible interpolation properties. This paper explores the continued evolution of this approach, examining its behavior when used to approximate a non-interpolable differential equation. We establish that the continuous phase evolution of runge-kutta methods for such equations is determined solely by the discrete solution values at the grid points. This fundamental connection leads to a novel integral formula that expresses the continuous phase evolution as a weighted sum of the discrete solution values and their associated rates of change. Building on this discovery, we derive an explicit formula for the continuous phase derivative. This new relationship enables the development of runge-kutta schemes that precisely reproduce the solution trajectories on any given grid. Moreover, for the specific case of the algebraic Riccati equation, we establish a formula for the continuous phase evolution that can be computed explicitly via Riccati recursion. This approach gives rise to a stochastic approximation algorithm for solving the continuous-time algebraic Riccati equation, along with an analysis of its asymptotic convergence. The introduction of fictitious forces allows the methods developed here to be extended to the solution of stochastic differential equations, which enables the construction of runge-kitty schemes for solving such equations and leads to an analysis of their asymptotic convergence. The theoretical findings presented in this work are substantiated through a range of numerical experiments that test their precision and convergence. The proposed methods are implemented in a companion Python package called CosmoPy that provides a comprehensive toolkit for their use. The package has already proven useful in a range of real-world applications, as illustrated by its introduction in the preliminary work that this paper draws on. The methods introduced here enjoy even broader applicability due to their precise interpolation properties and can be applied in fields such as astronomy and geophysics, along with numerous other domains. Our approach relies on training lightweight evaluation models to accurately replicate the performance of full-sized neural networks, which we subsequently validate through comprehensive experimentation across three practical use cases from the cybersecurity field. Our results show that RET not only enhances the evaluation of MPL models but also facilitates the deployment of these models in limited-resource systems, all while reducing the computational overhead by nearly double. Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this study, we model three-dimensional chaotic scattering using the three-dimensional Henon-Heiles system, a quasi-integrable model that exhibits Wada basins. Extending the principles of quasi-integration to three dimensions, we identify nonchaotic Wada basins that persist even in the absence of quasi-integration. However, our simulations reveal that these Wada basins emerge and evolve robustly when feeble dissipation is introduced, contrasting the behavior of typical Wada basins found in two-dimensional chaotic scattering which collapse under any level of dissipation. This unexpected outcome motivates further research into three-dimensional chaotic dynamics, particularly the roles of quasi-integration and dissipation in three-dimensional chaotic systems. Moreover, our results illustrate the potential for nonquasi-integration and dissipation to enhance Wada basin formation, a phenomenon that may be observed in various three-dimensional dynamical systems. Lastly, our results demonstrate the interplay between these two distinct mechanisms - quasi-integration and dissipation - and warrant further exploration into the underlying dynamics, offering new insights and perspectives for researchers. This study may stimulate novel approaches to analyze three-dimensional chaotic systems and their anomalous features. Finally, our results offer a new interpretation of the quasi-integration mechanism from a geometric and topological context. In this regard, our research may contribute to the ongoing efforts to elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving Wada basins and related anomalous phenomena in three-dimensional chaotic systems. This contribution may pave the way for future innovations in nonlinear dynamics, ultimately advancing our knowledge of this field. Moreover, our results are expected to propel research in related areas such as topological quantum physics, which may also benefit from these findings. This potential interaction between two previously disparate fields - nonlinear dynamics and topological quantum physics - may facilitate significant discoveries and insights in both fields. This potential collaboration may enable researchers to leverage knowledge and techniques from one area to advance the other, potentially leading to breakthroughs and new research avenues that have yet to be explored. This potential for cross-fertilization may enable novel contributions to the study of Wada basins and related phenomena, which are of significant interest in both nonlinear dynamics and topological quantum physics. This exchange of ideas and approaches may lead to unexpected and interesting results, including new insights into the quasi-integration mechanism and Wada basins that are specific to three-dimensional chaotic systems and their underlying dynamics. The production of light bosons with unusual properties under variations in electroweak symmetry is an essential aspect of many theoretical models. These bosons can interact with matter through taste channels such as electromagnetic, weak nuclear, and neutral pion interactions. In this research, we explore the creation of light bosons that can interact with matter through all four tastes. We also examine the conditions necessary for these bosons to remain stable for extended periods. We calculated the cross-section for the production of these bosons in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV through next-to-leading order partonic processes. The findings indicate that taste-altering light bosons can be produced at sufficient rates with detectable signals. Additionally, we determined the likelihood of detecting these bosons within specified data sets from the Large Hadron Collider. The research reveals that taste-altering light bosons that can interact through all four tastes are produced at higher rates when they can also decay into neutral pions or gamma-rays. The LHC can detect these bosons within certain data sets with up to ten thousand times the standard model predictions. The research also demonstrates that taste-aluring light bosons that can interact through all four tastes but also decay into neutral pions or gamma-rays can't survive for extended periods. The phase-space regions that contribute to the production and decay of these bosons result in undesirable autocorrelations, ultimately leading to undetectable and short-lived particles. The research specifically analyzes the effects of light bosons that can interact through all four tastes on neutrino oscillations and the associated LHC detection potential. The findings indicate that taste-aluring bosons that can interact through all four tastes but also decay into neutral pions or gamma-rays don't impact neutrino oscillations, whereas those that can interact through all four tastes without decaying into neutral pions or gamma-rays can impact neutrino oscillations. The research states that taste-aluring bosons that can interact through all four tastes without decaying into neutral pions or gamma-rays can't survive for extended periods. The LHC can detect these bosons within specified data sets with up to ten thousand times the standard model predictions. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved activity recognition performance in videos. Despite this progress, recognizing activities within short video clips of varying lengths remains a difficult task. To tackle this problem, we introduce a novel hierarchical model, the Focus Network, which incorporates a compact token attention mechanism and a predictive attention feature extractor. This innovative approach enables the Focus Network to effectively analyze sequences of images and temporal information within individual clips. By doing so, it achieves remarkable accuracy in activity recognition within both short and long video clips. Our model's efficacy is further validated by its ability to recognize activities in videos with missing frames and videos with uneven durations. Our research is further bolstered by a newly created dataset, the ActivityDataset, comprising 13,789 videos annotated with human-focused activity information. This dataset is peculiar as it is comprised of videos that are 5 to 40 frames long, making it significantly different from existing datasets. As such, it presents a unique set of challenges and complexities that are distinct from other annotation paradigms. To showcase the diversity of this dataset, we presented it as a set of videos displaying different aspects of daily life, all of which are centered around specific activities. Our model is highly versatile and can be applied to various activity recognition tasks within videos. To demonstrate its efficacy in real-world scenarios, we tested our model on two renowned datasets, JHMDB and 50Salms. Our model significantly improved the state-of-the-art performance on these datasets, achieving notable gains in accuracy and evaluation measures. Our research is a significant advancement in the field of vision-based activity recognition, primarily due to the unique Focus Network architecture and our creation of the ActivityDataset. Both of these components present novel solutions to longstanding problems in the field. As such, our research is a significant contribution to the study of vision-based activity recognition. To facilitate future research, we was cautious about introducing new variables and instead built upon existing ones. We also ensured that our model is data-efficient and not dependent on vast resources to train. Our data creation process was thoughtful as we aimed to present a dataset that is diverse and presents activities from a human perspective. Our model is a significant advancement in the field of vision-based activity recognition and we believe it will be a valuable tool for future research. Prior studies have demonstrated that adding a scalar field to RN-AdS black holes results in the formation of probe charged regular black holes under specific conditions. These regular black holes possess a maximum extent of extremality when the coupling reaches a critical point, thereby validating the feeble cosmic censorship hypothesis. Furthermore, the temperature of these regular black holes exhibits a null, infinite value at the point of extremality, signifying a highly unusual thermodynamic characteristic. While the free energy of the regular black holes indicates a maximum extent of extremality, it does not support the alternative interpretation of the feeble cosmic censorship hypothesis in terms of thermodynamic stability. Additionally, we have investigated the extension of the results to higher-dimensional scenarios, confirming the robustness of the findings. Nonetheless, the regularity of the solution when the scalar field coupling exceeds the critical value remains a topic of ongoing debate. We theorize that the regularity of the solution may be attributed to the inadequacy of the model in describing the interior structure of the black hole due to its probe nature. Moreover, the presence of a zero-point fluctuation contribution to the free energy in the adiabatic process could also pose a problem for the thermodynamic stability of the regular black holes. These findings suggest that the feeble cosmic censorship hypothesis may be challenged when considering the scenario of a black hole and a weak cosmic censorship in the context of RN-AdS black holes with scalar field coupling. Instead, the results offer novel insights into the feeble cosmic censorship hypothesis, particularly its relation to thermodynamics, and shed light on the regularity of singularities in black holes. Moreover, the results may also be related to holographic cosmic censorship, an concept that has garnered significant interest in the field of holographic theories. These findings could have significant implications for the understanding of the feeble cosmic censorship hypothesis in general relativity and holographic theories, particularly in the context of RN-AdS black holes with scalar field coupling. Moreover, the results may also be extended to consider scenarios involving quantum corrections to the black holes, such as those involving Myers-Poulton black holes and cubic scalar field theories coupled to RN-AdS black holes. Building on previous work, we broaden the definition of solutions for a general nonlinear hyperbolic conservation equation to include measure-valued solutions. To achieve this, we develop a novel approach using a specific type of measure that can be broken down into the sum of a diffeomorphism and a measure that vanishes outside a given compact set. This definition is consistent with the existing definition of solutions for nonlinear hyperbolic conservation equations, which is primarily applicable to diffeomorphisms, as well as a corresponding L1 theory for scalar equations. In addition, we establish that measure-valued solutions for systems of conservation laws are subject to certain conditions and constraints. This research is a progression of previously unpublished work by the second author and offers an alternative perspective on the existing results in the field. Furthermore, we examine the well-posedness of the initial value problem for measure-valued solutions, demonstrating certain limitations on their differentiability. Finally, we apply the measure-valued framework to a model known as the Chaplygin gas equation, which describes the behavior of a gas with a specific type of energy relation and is characterized by a singular shock that emerges in a limiting process. This model is an addition to the existing research on gas dynamics, which primarily focuses on solutions for Lagrangian partial differential equations. These investigations also have broader implications and connections to various fields, including geometry, analysis, and PDEs. In particular, we examine the geometric structure and properties of measure-valued solutions, which can be interpreted as geodesics on a specific type of manifold and are characterized by a variational principle, as well as the relationship between measure-valued solutions and probability measures, which is a key area of research in stochastic analysis and probability theory. This study also touches on other topics, such as the duality theory and second-order effects that arise in certain models, as well as the development of a semigroup action that regulates the behavior of measure-valued solutions over time. To conclude, we present several open questions and directions for future research, highlighting potential avenues for exploration and investigation. Notably, we examine the extension of the semigroup action to the space of measure-valued solutions, as well as the structure and properties of the limit measure that forms as time goes to infinity, which is a key area of research in analysis, geometry, and PDEs, as well as stochastic processes and probability theory. This research introduces NBcoded, a lightweight machine learning-based network assault detection system designed for resource-constrained devices. Comprising an encoder and a Naive Bayes classifier, NBcoded can operate effectively on devices with limited resources. To enhance its accuracy, a novel feature construction method is implemented using traffic pattern analysis. This involves generating distinct binary features for specific traffic parameters through an encoder, which are then used to train a Naive Bayes classifier. Our study evaluates NBcoded using the KDD Cup 99 and 2001 datasets, comparing its performance to existing detection methods. Notably, NBcoded outperforms alternative solutions by achieving up to a 5% higher accuracy rate, along with significantly lower computational complexity and memory requirements. Consequently, NBcoded is suited for operation on resource-constrained devices. An intrinsic property of a finite group's architecture and its prime-powered subdivisions is its expansion width, defined as the least integer $n$ such that the group's representations over a finite field of order 'q' cannot be reasonably equivalent when 'n' is greater than or equal to the number of divisions, and 'q' is less than or equal to the number of divisions. We identify the complete collection of finite groups with their expanded width equal to 'n', for 'n' equal to '1' and '2'. We demonstrate that subgroups of a specific type within a finite group and a related double coset are accountable for certain characteristics of the group's structure when 'n' is equal to '1'. We use this understanding to tackle a previously elusive problem, revealing whether a finite group's structure is determined entirely by its double coset structure. In another significant achievement, we identify the complete collection of finite groups with their expanded width equal to '1'. We demonstrate that a finite group's double coset structure can be simplified into a more manageable structure consisting of its Sylow subgroups and a specific configuration of double cosets, in cases where 'n' is equal to or greater than '4'. Finally, in a related area, we study a new concept called activity expansion, an concept related to a group's double cosets, and use it to resolve a long-standing open problem in group theory, and identify the complete collection of finite groups with their activity expansion equal to '1'. We demonstrate that a finite group's properties can be simplified into a more manageable structure consisting of its Sylow subgroups and a specific configuration of double cosets, in cases where the group's activity expansion is greater than or equal to '4'. We also show that certain characteristics of a finite group's structure are determined entirely by its double cosets, and provide a simplified representation of these characteristics, which can then be used to recover the entire group structure, for a wide range of finite groups known as solvable groups. In recent years, computational biologists have become deeply interested in understanding living organisms through visual analysis. By utilizing established machine learning methods, such as optical flow, for tracking biological movements in video footage has become a commonly adopted approach. However, we take a different perspective, developing a novel algorithm specifically designed for detecting and distinguishing biological movements within video footage. Our approach integrates the use of occlusion detection, both locally and globally, to refine and enhance the accuracy of movement identification. Furthermore, we incorporate a versatile similarity measure and a dynamic correlation analysis to effectively categorize the different movements present in the footage. Our proposed method demonstrates exceptional performance, with a high accuracy rate of 97.3%, 10% better than the current state-of-the-art. To validate our approach, we used publicly available taxonomic classifications of Drosophila melanogaster wing movements and successfully mapped out the genetic influence on the expression of such movements. Our novel algorithm thus not only facilitates the identification and classification of biological movements but also reveals the underlying genetic mechanisms influencing those movements. Our research provides a robust framework for the analysis of complex biological data through a machine learning-based approach. To ensure full transparency and reproducibility, we have made accessible both our algorithm and the computational tools we developed for this research, available at https://github.com/CDS-IRQL/BioMotion. Our study has the potential for wide applications in the field of computational biology, particularly for understanding and interpreting the movement patterns of animals. We have applied our algorithm to the analysis of Drosophila melanogaster wing movements but due to technical restrictions we cannot show videos. Our approach, however, is highly versatile and can be applied to any system or organism based on video footage. We envision extensive applications of our research in the fields of evolution, neurobiology, medicine, and conservation, among others. Achieving this goal viable and sustainable requires upgrading the energy infrastructure to maintain system reliability and meet increasing energy demands. Current methods for assessing and optimizing energy networks rely on traditional mathematical techniques, but these approaches often fail to consider the interactions between different energy sectors and the uncertainty associated with future demand and supply conditions. Furthermore, these methods are prone to computational difficulties as problem sizes increase. In contrast, recent breakthroughs in quantum computing technology have opened the door for incorporating novel optimization techniques, like quantum inspired algorithms, into critical decision-making processes for energy management. In our research, we show how quantum-inspired techniques can be utilized to enhance energy infrastructure and improve the efficiency of different energy systems, including electric, gas, heat, and air-conditioning systems. Our experiments using real-world data from Germany and New York reveal that quantum-inspired methods can significantly reduce computational costs associated with large-scale problems, up to $10^{3}$ times for some tests, while producing near-optimal solutions that outperform classical methods. Our results indicate that quantum-inspired methods are suitable for practical applications in energy infrastructure management and could be further developed for tackling other complex problems in advanced data analysis. Ultimately, we believe that the rapid advancement in quantum technology will enable us to solve problems previously intractable due to their high computational complexity, thus enabling more precise and efficient planning of energy systems with considerations for reliability, efficiency, and environmental impact. In particular, we have explored the potential of using quantum-inspired techniques to model and analyze various concepts in energy systems, such as gas lift, gas-driven wells, and demand response, which are now becoming popular in modern energy management methods. By applying these techniques, we can incorporate the effects of supply and demand uncertainty and account for the non-linear interactions between different energy sectors, something which traditional mathematical methods often struggle to handle. Our results show that quantum-inspired methods can lead to improved efficiency and reduced costs in energy systems, and with advancements in quantum technology, we can develop more sophisticated models and algorithms for tackling complex problems in energy management. A fundamental concept underlying physical laws lies in the self-dual nature of information, which has two aspects: the quantitative aspect relating to bits and Boolean algebra, and the qualitative aspect involving symbols and semantic meaning. This duality allows for the exploration of global principles governing physical laws through the analysis of information properties. From a quantitative perspective, physical systems can be seen as information systems with constraints, which brings us to the study of information dynamics and the universal laws governing physical systems. Despite breakthroughs in this field, widespread adoption of information-based approaches to physics is hindered by a lack of coherence. To rectify this, we use formal semantics and algebraic systems to reveal underlying invariants, which can serve as the foundation for developing a unified theory of physical systems based on information. This approach allows us to investigate the consistency of existing physical theories within a broader framework and identify inconsistencies, which can lead to novel experimental predictions and research directions. It is hoped that this method will stimulate more conversations among physicists with information-theoretic backgrounds. Additionally, we see an opportunity for information theory to shape and guide new research in physics, leading to novel discoveries and insights. Acoustic wave methods in solids are commonly used to determine the dynamics of lattice vibrations and of coupled solid-liquid systems.  One specific technique, called Brillouin light scattering, has been widely applied while a lesser-known method, called controllable acoustic strain spectroscopy, has distinct benefits of its own, albeit primarily studied in isolated systems so far.  Our research group recently used this latter technique to study the dynamics of water coupled with a channelled wall, an arrangement that offers both experimental accessibility and theoretical complexity.  By doing so, we've discovered new insights into how water interacts with a non-flat surface at a nanoscale level.  Our data reveals two distinct regimes of water dynamics - one controlled by the channel size and the other by the frequency of the waves - and reveals an intermediate 'boson summit' where water's dynamic behavior is nearly indistinguishable from that of a solid.  By combining these findings with computer simulations, we've gained a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms, including how water's 'frozen' patterns arise from fluctuations that match the shape of the containing walls.  Our study suggests a universal principle that can be applied to other confined systems as well.  Additionally, we've noted an intriguing connection between our findings and the behavior of glassy systems, and propose that our data, along with future neutron scattering studies, may reveal that the boson summit is actually close to room temperature.  Our research provides a significant foundation for future research into the dynamics of nanoscale systems, particularly through the application of strain spectroscopy.  To prove it, we've developed an extensive research plan that includes both experiments and theoretical studies, focusing on key areas such as coupled water-protein dynamics, protein freezing and the related structural changes in proteins that may occur due to fluctuation-induced effects, and finally the broad class of glassy systems comprising both biological and man-made materials.  Our goal is to uncover the widespread occurrence of the boson summit principle in nature.  By doing so, we may also be able to design materials that have novel and freeze-like properties just a short distance from room temperature.  Additionally, we see great potential for a novel medical therapy approach that uses strain oscillations to destroy cancer cells by pushing them beyond their boson summit limit.  Our project, called 'Cryothermia,' may offer a promising treatment option that has thus far not been fully exploited. Achieving practical quantum simulations is considered a major milestone for emulating complex quantum systems on a smaller scale. By integrating analog and digital quantum computing techniques, we've developed a new hybrid approach for approximating the quantum states of fermionic systems. This hybrid method combines analog quantum circuits with the digital quantum computer's ability to precisely measure interactions, without the need for precise individual gate operations that are challenging to control. Instead, we've devised a method to leverage analog-phased interactions, utilizing randomness to screen and filter outcomes on a digital level. This hybrid approach, utilizing fewer qubits than analog methods, allows us to accurately simulate the fermionic system's behavior. Furthermore, our experiments have demonstrated the efficacy of this technique by successfully emulating a fermionic system on a 12-qubit hybrid quantum computer. This development not only presents an accessible path to simulating complex materials but also serves as a vital precursor to utilizing noisy, on-demand quantum computers for digital computing applications. Additionally, our findings suggest that hybrid quantum computers may possess an essential advantage over analog counterparts, given their potential to connect analog-phased interactions with reliable measurement capabilities. This could pave the way for emulating complex fermionic systems on a larger scale. Lastly, our research also uncovered an unexpected connection between quantum simulations and quantum cryptography, specifically highlighting the distinct characteristics needed to distinguish these two applications, which further informs our quest for reliable, accurate quantum simulations. By achieving this, we may also break through to a deeper understanding of the underlying quantum physics that governs complex materials and reactions. This research was supported through grants from the Basic Science Research Program, the Quantum Coordinated Research Program, and the Industrial Strategy Team. Achieving the precise control of light across various applications, such as tissue engineering and gene therapy, necessitates a sophisticated light modulation system capable of delivering high-resolution, high-stability projection. While current solutions, including digital micro-mirror devices and liquid crystals, offer excellent resolution, they fall short in meeting the high frame-rate and high persistence requirements for tissue applications. In contrast, ferroelectric liquid crystals offer a suitable alternative due to their high contrast ratios, fast response times, and flexibility for large-area applications. Nonetheless, their conventional control using binary ferroelectric liquid crystals may not suffice for intricate tissue patterns. This study proposes an innovative iterative framework that leverages a binary ferroelectric liquid crystal system in conjunction with a single-layer ferroelectric crystal display, enhancing the crystal's gray-scale capabilities. This enhancement, combined with our novel control algorithm, allows for high-resolution, high-stability image projection, a feat that can potentially be adapted for tissue applications. We have successfully tested and demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed method through a series of experiments. Our innovative structure, designed to iterate between binary and gray-scale FLC states, has shown promising results, with a 32x32 SLM achieving 8 gray-scale levels and a 64x64 SLM reaching 6 gray-scale levels, both with excellent uniformity and high persistence. These findings indicate that our solution can create intricate tissue-like patterns with a high level of resolution, paving the way for innovative applications in tissue engineering and gene therapy. Additionally, our study highlights the feasibility of using a single uniform alloyed ferroelectric liquid crystal to create a gray-scale ferroelectric crystal display, a feature that can potentially be utilized in various display applications. Moreover, our iterative approach offers a versatile solution for adapting binary FLC systems to produce gray-scale images, with a high level of flexibility that could be applied to a range of ferroelectric crystal display technologies. We have also successfully demonstrated the functionality of our proposed algorithm using a 64x64 binary FLC system, achieving a high level of resolution and persistence, and achieving a high level of gray-scale resolution in our experimental results. These breakthroughs stem from our innovative iterative framework that integrates the benefits of binary and gray-scale ferroelectric liquid crystals, and we believe that our solution will contribute significantly to the development of next-generation light modulation systems. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, we investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a monolithic demonstrator with small collection electrodes. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and the size of the sensitive area. Various test silicon substrates with different thermal histories and grown epitaxial layers are examined. In addition to silicon substrates, InGaAs sensors are also studied for their CMOS image sensors' potential in particle physics applications. The charge collection properties, active sensor depth, and sensitive area size are investigated for both monolithic and detector-specific designs. The active sensor depth is determined using two methods, one-based on the beam scan and another based on the temperature and resistivity dependence. The results of these investigations, along with the characteristics of CLICTD devices, are presented and discussed. In this research, we have discovered that monolithic CMOS sensors feature a significant portion of the sensitive area along the length of the wafer. The active sensor depth has been found to correlate with the epitaxial layer thickness, a key factor influencing CMOS sensor design. The InGaAs sensors, suitable for infrared detection, also exhibit a substantial sensitive area. The charge collection properties of these sensors show great potential for use in infrared detectors in particle physics experiments. The use of thin active detectors could provide improved sensitivity and higher event detection capabilities. The implementation of shallow p-type dopant layers or tailored thermal treatments could significantly enhance the charge collection properties. A deep high-quality epitaxial layer would be beneficial for both silicon and InGaAs sensors, allowing for an optimal design of the detector-substrate structure and potentially leading to better results. The formation of a thin high-quality layer on silicon and InGaAs substrates using a specific thermal treatment could significantly improve the charge collection properties and increase the active sensor depth. The technique has been found to be effective and could be applied to monolithic CMOS sensors to improve their charge collection properties and increase the active sensor depth. The method could be widely utilized across the industry to produce high-quality detector-substrate structures and increase the active sensor depth. The novel concept of a shallow p-type dopant layer or a deep high-quality epitaxial layer could lead to a significant breakthrough in detector design and potentially expand the scope of monolithic CMOS detectors, enabling the detection of more particles

Advanced telescopes like the Extremely Large Telescope may benefit from a cutting-edge technology called Rapid Atmospheric Self-coherent Camera (RASCJ). This innovative approach identifies and eliminates the impact of speckles in high-resolution images by directly removing the distortions introduced by the remaining speckles on the focal plane. We have successfully tested RASCJ on a testbed at the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Facility and achieved remarkable results, specifically focusing on the control of speckle velocities. Our experiments showed that RASCJ effectively controls speckles with velocities up to 600 meters per second and retains over 90% of the original image's brightness, demonstrating its potential to enhance the performance of future astronomical observations. This technique may become a crucial component of future ground-based astronomical observations and play a key role in enhancing the performance of the Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics system. Our experiments not only verified the viability of RASCJ but also revealed the necessity of further research to fully explore the potential of this ground-breaking technology. We have found that speaking of RASCJ at the level of subrotations (speckle diameter equivalent to 100 nanometers or less) is more feasible and promising compared to speaking of it at the level of macrotations (speckle diameter equivalent to 1000 nanometers or more). Moreover, exploring the trade-offs between algorithm complexity and performance will be an important direction for further study. Ultimately, we have determined that RASCJ has the capability to significantly enhance the high-resolution image quality that telescopes can achieve. Still, we will need to conduct more specific observations on the speckles present in the atmosphere to fully understand its potential and effectively implement it in high-resolution astronomical imaging. To that end, we have outlined a plan for subsequent experiments that include the implementation of a 64-element camera array to directly test the RASCJ approach on the speakers we have already established. Moreover, we will conduct these experiments under more challenging conditions that mimic the speckle distribution in the atmosphere, specifically looking into the trade-offs between focusing on either speckles with uniform distribution or those with a more complex distribution that better represents the speckle pattern in the atmosphere. Once we have successfully tested these experiments, we will then work on refining the algorithm and implementing a more robust version of the RASCJ code. Furthermore, we will also explore the possibility of using a more advanced hardware and software system that utilizes 169 speakers and explores the potential of using a more focused approach on specific parts of the speakers.

This study presents a novel variant of the combined Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, known as the CIS, which aims to address the potential issues of negative interest rates that have become a common phenomenon in the current economic climate. The interest rate process is modified to ensure it remains non-negative by adopting a determinant approach. The model's success in preventing negative interest rates is evaluated through two key aspects: its ability to fit well with real market data and its capacity to generate realistic outcomes. The study examines the distinct characteristics of different specification variants of the model and their performance when applied to two separate datasets, namely the US and UK bond prices, as well as a joint analysis of the US and UK yield curves. The empirical results indicate that the proposed model exhibits superior performance in terms of both predictive power and accuracy. Additionally, the study conducts a formal goodness-of-fit test to compare the performance of different model variants, revealing that the proposed determinant-shift model exhibits higher probabilities of passing this test. The associated simulation results confirm the empirical findings, underscoring the importance of considering non-negative constraints in the context of interest rate models. Based on the empirical results and the good performance of the proposed model, particularly its variant known as CIS-2, this study offers practical recommendations for the practical application of this model in real-world scenarios. The proposed model can be utilized as a reliable tool for generating simulated data and providing expert opinions in operations research, as well as other potential applications. The associated MATLAB code for generating simulated data is provided, allowing for precise replication of the model's output. The study provides a comprehensive theoretical examination of the model's properties, commencing with a detailed analysis of the conditions required for the model's parameters to be unique and adaptable. The study further demonstrates that the proposed model can be accurately estimated using both ordinary least squares and maximum likelihood methods. The associated simulation results confirm the empirical findings, revealing that the model's estimated parameters exhibit relatively small and consistent errors when applied to both small and large sample sizes. The study concludes by highlighting the key distinctives of the proposed model, which is poised to become a valuable asset in the field of econometric research, particularly when modeling non-negative interest rates in the current economic climate. The proposed model can be a valuable tool for maintaining stationarity and ensuring negative interest rates in the context of continuous-time models, which is a significant contribution to the existing literature on Cox-Ingersoll-Ross models and their variants. The study provides a comprehensive comparison with other existing models, which it distinguishes from the proposed determinant-shift model

This study proposes a novel integration method to handle the collisions between particles in particle-resolved simulations of non-Newtonian fluids. Unlike fixed-time-step methods that update simulation data constantly, this new method employs different time steps for fluid particles and suspended particles. Initially, fluid particles are updated using the finite volume method at regular, predetermined time intervals. Collisions between particles trigger updates for all involved particles using a smaller time step until the completion of all collisions. Subsequent updates of fluid particles use a average time step that takes into account the varying collision durations. Through the simulation of a colliding pair of particles, we observed that using larger fluid particles can accommodate longer collision durations without noticeably affecting the particles' velocities after the collision. Furthermore, this method has accelerated the particle-resolved simulation of a non-Newtonian fluid by up to two times over a fixed-time-step method. Consequently, this method has successfully reduced the computational burden in particle-resolved simulations that incorporate realistic collision durations. Nonetheless, the method still experiences an increase in computational cost due to the increased number of updates, particularly for dilute suspensions undergoing a large number of collisions. An optimization technique has been suggested to mitigate this issue. Through the analysis of a settling particle demonstration, we have observed that the new integration method can successfully simulate complex collisions and are confident that this method will contribute positively to the field of particle-resolved simulations. Additionally, we believe that this method can be adapted and utilized in diverse types of simulations, such as those involving non-Newtonian fluids and colloidal mixtures. Our results indicate that the BEC rule does not universally apply in metals, as it does in insulators. However, we find that the nonadiabatic Born effective coefficient can be expressed as a ratio of values representing the linear displacement of the electrons' charge density to the lattice displacement, but this ratio is only meaningful when the lattice displacement is not confined within a single unit cell. Since metals by definition have no energy gap at zero energy and an infinite number of states at the Fermi level, calculating the BEC in metals poses unique challenges. In our model, we used a finite electron system with periodic boundary conditions and found that the effective charge is dependent on the system's size and shape. Currently, there is no well-defined method to calculate the effective charge for an infinite electron system in metals. Our results indicate that the BEC rule can be an useful approximation in metals for specific phonon modes where the electron charge response is localized within a single unit cell, and we provide a criterion to assess this localization. Additionally, we find that the BEC in metals is related to the Drude mass, which is a parameter used in the Drude model of conductivity to simulate the response of electrons to a external electric field, and we derive this relationship theoretically. Our work indicates that the BEC in metals can be calculated more easily than in insulators due to its connection with the Drude mass, and we suggest that the Drude mass could be a useful alternative to the effective charge in modeling the nonadiabatic interaction between electrons and lattice in metals. Furthermore, we used our results to estimate the effective charge for the stable and metastable phonon modes in a simple cubic structure, and we found that these effective charges show symmetry behavior. We establish two distinct types of denotational semantics for the probabilistic lambda-calculus. Initially based on classical and intuitionistic probability theory, our framework can also be refined for using non-standard methods. By contrast to existing approaches which often rely on Markov chains or other discrete-time models, our proposed semantics provides a continuous-time framework that is in line with the underlying calculus, enabling a more intuitive understanding of the calculus. Moreover, we demonstrate that the probabilistic lambda-calculus is equipped with a strong form of fidelity, a concept essential for the theoretical foundation of quantum programming. To develop this, we draw upon the ideas of Kleisli categories and adjunctions, extending the intuitionistic version of Sottile's category-theoretic lifting framework to the context of probabilistic lambda-calculus. Finally, we showcase the relevance of our non-standard semantics by describing a probabilistic lambda-calculus realisation of the Well-Pinned Monte Carlo method for estimating the pinned energy in polymer science. This example illustrates the versatility of probabilistic lambda-calculus in tackling inexact optimization problems in science. In particular, we refine the non-standard semantics of the calculus to accommodate the specific requirements of the Well-Pinned Monte Carlo algorithm. By doing so, we move a step forward towards the quantum foundation of such algorithms, a goal closely related to the broader quest of quantumifying the foundations of modern science. This work is a continuation of my PhD dissertation, fully presented in my conference paper titled 'Probabilistic lambda-calculus: from quantum-inspired to quantum-compatible (and perhaps quantum-enabled) programming', which was defended on July 7, 2022. In this dissertation, I explored the probabilistic lambda-calculus as a strategy for approaching quantum programming, while also investigating the insights and insights-gaps that arise from applying this approach. One of the key goals of my research is to study quantum-inspired and quantum-compatible programming as a valuable means of fostering investigative and reflective attitudes towards quantum programming, even if it means not entirely enabling it. By examining the fundamental quantum-programming problems that emerge through the lens of the probabilistic lambda-calculus, I hope to shed light on the inherent challenges and limitations of quantum programming, while also highlighting its unique opportunities for facilitating innovative and groundbreaking applications of quantum computing. In particular, my research focuses on understanding how the probabilistic lambda-calculus, with its continuous-time framework and strong form of fidelity, relates to established quantum algorithms and practical quantum programming problems, such as the quantum approximation of non-symmetric operators and the implementation of the Born rule

In software design, natural language-based requirements gathering is both crucial and challenging.
The manual process of analyzing design conversations is difficult and error-prone.
Existing research, while promising, has not resolved this issue.
This paper addresses the question of how to apply patterns in design conversations to guide the mining of relevant information.
Using an automated approach called Conclusion Stability, we evaluate natural language-based design conversation mining models and assess their reliability.
Our method analyzes the consistent conclusions drawn from design discussions regarding a specific software component and evaluates how often these conclusions appear when new, unseen discussions are applied to the model.
The higher the consistency, the more reliable the model in reflecting the actual user thoughts and the better it performs in summarizing design conversations.
Our approach Conclusion Stability, demonstrates good performance in evaluating design conversation mining models and provides valuable insights for developers, revealing discrepancies between code comments and actual design conversations that can improve system design and user experience.
Our experiment with 180 Java classes from the Neuro-Symbol library proves Conclusion Stability's effectiveness in analyzing design conversations, showing a significant correlation of 0.71 between consistency and accuracy, and surpassing traditional metrics such as precision and recall in evaluating design conversation mining models.
Our study also highlights the diversity of design conversations that can inform software development and the potential applications of Conclusion Stability in other natural language-based software engineering tasks. We aim to tackle this issue through the development of an innovative, template-matching method based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). This technique is capable of being executed in a highly efficient, parallelized manner using graphics processing units (GPUs). Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits superior accuracy and resistance to noise compared to the current fastest techniques. Our work not only presents a highly optimized implementation but also an open-source software tool, called Astrophotonic, which is based on the successful model, allowing the community to benefit from our findings. However, they have not considered how adapting might impact data that has been labeled as fine in the originating area.  In the United States, this issue becomes even more critical.  Since driving standards change significantly from country to country, even minor shifts in environment are reflected in statistical patterns of the traffic flow and road conditions.  Moreover, there are more varied types of road hazards in the U.S. compared to the rest of Europe, resulting in even more significant differences between the originating and adapting domains.  Consequently, there's a need for methods that not only improve adapting area performance but also maintain or even improve model performance in the originating area.  This research introduces a statistical method that utilizes two contrasting loss functions to achieve this goal by balancing transferring learning with preserving labeled data in the originating area. Association rule discovery is a crucial step in market basket analysis and other applications. The extensive search space for these rules can be diminished by confining attention to itemsets that include infrequent patterns, effectively narrowing down the search parameters. The process involves two key steps: generating potential association rules and validating their significance. The significance assessment stage can be achieved through various methods, some of which have a proven track record, while others are relatively untested. The choice of validation method has an impact on the final association rule output and the resulting sizes of the minimal-size bases (MSB) resulting from different choices, but surprisingly, some untested methods yield better results in this regard. We introduce a previously uninvestigated validation method called the union-confidence-union-coverage (UCUC) approach, which is an extension of the union-confidence-union (UCU) method introduced in 2003. The UCUC method has several advantages, including faster computation time, superior quality of the association rules, and the ability to provide the MSB with minimal-size bases of the association rules. Experiments using real-world data from the Udata benchmark dataset reinforce the effectiveness of the UCUC method. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of redundancy in association rules, including measures of redundancy, its impact on union and intersection results, and a novel algorithm for eliminating redundancy from itemsets while maintaining union and intersection results. The utility of this approach in data mining tasks is also illustrated. Lastly, we examine the relationship between the MSB, the union results, and the intersection results of association rules, and propose a novel definition of the MSB called the weak MSB, which is a generalization of the traditional MSB definition. The union results, intersection results, and weak MSB were also the focus of separate publications in 2013 and 2014, respectively. We have now proved that they are equivalent, and further refined this notion by demonstrating that the weak MSB is comprised of the largest union results, and also derived a formula for calculating the size of the weak MSB. The operational framework of the US criminal justice system necessitates the incorporation of health care and mental health care delivery mechanisms. Research indicates that approximately 1 in 5 adults experiencing symptoms of a serious mental illness and 14% of children and adolescents exhibit such symptoms. Studies have demonstrated the crucial role mental health care plays in promoting public safety, reducing crime rates, and promoting healthy communities, and have highlighted the effectiveness of therapy-based treatments in achieving these goals. To this end, several countries have introduced and implemented court-ordered therapy programs for individuals within the justice system, and studies have been conducted on their impact. Leveraging data from the National Survey of Patients in the Correctional System in the state of New York, we examine the effect of participating in a compulsory therapy program for incarcerated individuals, focusing on the type of therapy delivered, mode of delivery, and patient response. We find that participants exhibiting lower levels of psychological well-being, as measured by a 12-item well-being scale, are more likely to benefit from therapy-based treatments, and that the type of therapy delivered and patient response are key factors in determining treatment effectiveness. Furthermore, we identify the most effective therapeutic approaches, and uncover discontinuities in treatment efficacy among incarcerated individuals undergoing therapy, and find that the manner in which therapy is delivered, and patient characteristics, account for these disparities. Our analysis highlights the significance of tailoring mental health care delivery systems within the justice system to meet the unique needs and characteristics of patients, and that the most effective therapeutic approaches should be prioritized and implemented in order to promote public safety, reduce crime, and promote healthy communities. Radio cartography involves surveying the airspaces with various wireless communications systems to identify available channels for interference mitigation and capacity maximization. Recent advancements in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) technology has renewed interest in radio cartography. Our study examines the feasibility of autonomously generating radio maps using UAVs equipping only with basic wireless capabilities, without additional sensing instruments. We propose a novel approach called IndepUV, which uses channel sounding and a distributed average subgradient-based algorithm operating in parallel to estimate the radio map. Our analysis of IndepUV's convergence and stability properties is provided, and numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this method. Interestingly, the results show that the proposed approach can yield accurate outcomes using fewer UAVs than the minimum required for convergence and stability. Specifically, two UAVs are enough to accurately estimate a two-dimensional radio map using only basic wireless capabilities. We also found that deep learning techniques can enhance radio map estimation accuracy, particularly when UAVs have access to licensed channels. However, deep learning models may struggle to perform well in channel sounding-based methods and scenarios with limited system resources. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing novel deep learning-based approaches that can effectively utilize available system resources for radio map estimation. The proposed algorithms and methods are further supported by a functional demo, consisting of: (i) a web-based radio map visualization tool; (ii) a simulation environment for evaluating UAV strategies; (iii) a fully implemented radio cartography system using UAVs. The source code for these components is openly accessible on GitHub. By openly sharing our code and demos, we aim to facilitate further research and development in this area. Keywords: Radio cartography, UAVs, wireless communications, interference mitigation, capacity maximization, wireless localization, deep learning, simulation demo, open-source software.

A flexible fracture emerges in rafts when they are subjected to high levels of stretch, causing the material to divide into distinct islands. As a result, understanding the behavior and accuracy of predicting raft fracture becomes increasingly important for applications involving the use of soft and flexible materials. This article aims to enhance current knowledge of fracture by providing a comprehensive analysis of its occurrence, along with the introduction of a novel theoretical model that explains the material's breakage from multiple aspects. Additionally, we examine the effects of particle softness on fracture through detailed simulations, revealing how the material's breakage changes under different levels of strain for stiffer particles, while presenting an new approach for designing more robust and flexible materials. Our findings also open the door for further research on fracture, along with promising avenues for future applications and investigations. It's also worth mentioning that our work doesn't cover biological systems such as living tissues, as we specifically focus on the fracture of soft and elastic materials. Our study does, however, shed light on new paths for further research on both biological systems and other types of elastic materials. Finally, we explore potential ways to apply our knowledge to practical problems, such as improving material durability by learning from our findings on particle softness and its impact on fracture. Our work is complemented by an online repository containing additional data and code needed to replicate our results and build upon our research. This includes numerical models used to simulate and study the material's breakage, along with experimental methods for observing and analyzing raft fracture. This extra information can serve as a valuable resource for future research and collaborations, further enhancing our understanding of fracture and flexible materials. We hope our study contributes to a deeper knowledge of soft and elastic materials, while inspiring new research and applications. This new information can potentially lead to breakthroughs in various fields such as materials science, biology, and aerodynamics, among others. Our analysis shows that the material's properties are influenced by the degree of mismatch between the gallium nitride and the substrate, with significant improvements observed for small mismatches. Various experimental techniques were used to characterize the material, including X-ray diffraction, X-ray diffraction spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and photoluminescence spectroscopy. The findings of this study suggest that the material's properties are directly related to the degree of strain in the gallium nitride layer, which in turn is influenced by the choice of substrate material. A notable improvement in the material's luminescence was observed, with the highest quality samples exhibiting the longest wavelength and highest intensity of light emission. A maximum 5.5 times improvement in the material's luminescence was observed, along with significant reductions in the number of defects present. The structural modifications resulting from growing gallium nitride on these substrates have significant positive effects on the material's electrical and optical properties, making these combinations promising for the development of advanced semiconductor devices. The optimal combinations identified in this study could lead to significant reductions in energy loss in future gallium nitride-based devices. The observations of this study also provide valuable insights into how the material's crystal structure affects its electrical and optical properties, particularly the role of hole conductivity in gallium nitride. The novel gallium nitride materials discovered in this study could have important applications in quantum electronics, where hole conductivity is critical for the operation of devices. The development of these new materials could enable significant breakthroughs in quantum electronics, such as higher efficiency lasers and faster switches. The research of this study opens up new avenues for the development of advanced gallium nitride materials and paves the way for future innovations in quantum electronics. The novel gallium nitride materials discovered in this study also provide a valuable model for the development of other semiconductor materials, where strain and crystal structure can be used to enhance a material's electrical and optical properties. It demonstrates that the C*-algebra version of robust shift equivalence is equivalent to the C*-version of shift equivalence, and proves that two row-finite directed graphs are robustly shift equivalent if and only if their C*-algebras are shift equivalent. Additionally, it is shown that the notion of robust shift equivalence is broader than weak shift equivalence but not broader than strong shift equivalence within the context of finite graphs. Finally, a method is devised to construct a common covering of two C*-algebras from strongly shift equivalent graphs, and it is demonstrated that this construction can be employed in the infinite graph scenario if the shift equivalence is of a particular type. These results generalize and resolve a longstanding question about the relationship between strong and weak shift equivalence first proposed by Katsuda and Yasue. Identifying the atomic Rydberg states via optical transitions is challenging due to their low optical accessibility. We have developed a new method that leverages multifrequency microwave radiation to detect Rydberg states with high precision. This innovative technique involves modeling Rabi oscillations using a deep neural network that incorporates multiple frequencies, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately predicting Rydberg state probabilities. Furthermore, our method enables the extraction of key energy level coupling parameters, specifically Rabi frequencies and Stark shifts, thereby facilitating high-precision quantum control. We have successfully tested this technique in an experiment involving $^{40}$Rb atoms, demonstrating a $10^4$ enhancement in the sensitivity of detecting Rydberg states based on microwave mediation. This highly sensitive detection method could greatly aid the development of high precision quantum computing and quantum network applications. Additionally, our deep learning approach can be adapted to detect Rydberg states in diverse atomic species and may contribute to the exploration of quantum phenomena in diverse systems. We have released the trained models and relevant software tools for this purpose, making this technology accessible to the scientific community.
